chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Decade in the Making

The inflection that Lumentum Holdings had spent a decade positioning for arrived, without ceremony, in the fiscal year ended June 2025. Cloud-and-datacenter demand from hyperscaler AI deployments drove what management called "unprecedented" growth rates across the company's optical-interconnect portfolio, pulling segment revenue mix decisively away from the telecom hardware cycle that had defined the company's earlier years and toward the AI infrastructure build-out that now constitutes the central investment thesis.

Lumentum (ticker: LITE, NASDAQ) is headquartered in San Jose, California. It was spun out of JDS Uniphase in August 2015 alongside its sister company Viavi Solutions, which retained the network-test business. The separation left Lumentum as a focused optical components and subsystems franchise: commercially a pure-play on the photonic layer of the global communications stack, and structurally the principal listed Western merchant supplier of indium phosphide chips and coherent optical components in a market with limited merchant capacity globally.

Michael Hurlston became President and Chief Executive Officer in February 2025, succeeding Alan Lowe, who had led the company from its JDSU spin-off through a decade that included the Oclaro acquisition, the Apple 3D-sensing scaling, and the subsequent normalisation. Hurlston brought to the role a career that had included nineteen years at Broadcom — latterly as General Manager of Mobile Connectivity Products — followed by five years as CEO of Synaptics, where he executed a strategic pivot away from PC and mobile-touch toward IoT and edge AI. The brief at Lumentum was analogous in character: sharpen the strategic focus toward the highest-value growth market, which in this case meant cloud-and-datacenter optical interconnect at hyperscaler customers.

## Two Segments, One Growth Engine

Lumentum reports two operating segments. Cloud & Networking — the larger, incorporating transceivers, ROADMs, coherent components, and indium phosphide chips — is the segment absorbing hyperscaler AI capex. Industrial Tech, incorporating commercial lasers for materials processing and semiconductor manufacturing as well as the legacy VCSEL 3D-sensing product line, provides a secondary revenue base but has been a drag: Industrial Tech revenue contracted roughly 15 percent in fiscal 2025 as 3D-sensing volumes normalised off the Apple peak.

The acquisitive history that created today's Cloud & Networking capability unfolded in two steps. The December 2018 acquisition of Oclaro for approximately $1.8 billion brought indium phosphide vertical integration — Lumentum manufactures the InP wafers from which externally modulated laser (EML) chips are produced, a capability that fewer than a handful of companies globally possess at commercial scale. The August 2022 acquisition of NeoPhotonics for approximately $918 million layered in coherent transceiver intellectual property and engineering depth; Wupen Yuen, a senior engineering leader from NeoPhotonics, now runs cloud-and-networking engineering at Lumentum.

## From Trough to Inflection

The financial baseline against which the Hurlston-era is measured was a trough. Fiscal 2024 revenue came in at $1.36 billion — compressed from the $1.74 billion peak of fiscal 2023 by the simultaneous unwinding of post-Apple-VCSEL normalisation and a broad telecom hardware downturn. Gross margins contracted sharply on the volume deleverage.

The recovery that followed was driven almost entirely by one product: EML chips for 800G datacom transceivers deployed by hyperscalers in AI cluster interconnect. Fiscal 2025 revenue recovered to $1.645 billion, a gain of 21 percent, on Cloud & Networking revenues of $1.41 billion — 85.8 percent of the company total, up from a lower prior-year mix, and growing approximately 30 percent year-on-year. The fourth fiscal quarter, ended 28 June 2025, recorded total revenue of $480.7 million, with Cloud & Networking contributing $424.1 million, or 88 percent of the company total — a year-on-year gain of 67 percent in that segment. [Lumentum Q4 FY2025 press release, investor.lumentum.com](https://investor.lumentum.com/financial-news-releases/news-details/2025/Lumentum-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx)

| Period | Total Revenue | Cloud & Networking | % Mix |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | $1,359m | ~$1,085m | ~80% |
| FY2025 | $1,645m | $1,411m | 86% |
| Q4 FY2025 | $481m | $424m | 88% |
| Q1 FY2026 | $534m | n/a disclosed | — |

The momentum carried into fiscal 2026. First-quarter revenue, reported in November 2025, reached $533.8 million — up 58 percent year-on-year — against company guidance of $510–540 million. Hurlston set a public target of surpassing $600 million in quarterly revenue by the end of fiscal 2026.

## The EML Chokepoint

The specific product around which Lumentum's competitive advantage has crystallised is the EML chip — the laser at the heart of the 800G pluggable transceiver modules that hyperscalers deploy by the hundreds of thousands in AI-cluster spine-leaf fabrics. Lumentum claims roughly 50-60 percent of the global market for 200G line-speed EMLs, the component that steps up into 1.6T transceivers as customers migrate from 800G.

> "Demand is still outstripping supply on our EMLs." — *Michael Hurlston, Q3 FY2025 earnings call, May 2025*

The supply constraint reflects two structural factors: the capital intensity and yield difficulty of InP wafer fabrication, and what Hurlston described as a reliability and yield advantage in the field.

> "Customers typically report a significantly higher yield on their cloud modules using our EMLs over competitors. Our design is the best performing...allows us pricing latitude." — *Michael Hurlston, Q4 FY2025 earnings call, August 2025*

Management was explicit that the generation transition from 800G to 1.6T represented additive rather than substitutive demand. Asked whether 800G volumes would fade as 1.6T ramped, Hurlston's answer was direct:

> "There's no transition, you know, down and up kind of situation. It's layered on top of." — *Michael Hurlston, Q4 FY2025 earnings call*

By the fourth fiscal quarter of 2025, EML shipments had nearly doubled year-on-year, hitting an all-time high. A substantial order for 200G-line-speed EML chips — destined for 1.6T transceiver modules — was booked, with fill expected in the December 2025 quarter. Lumentum also recognised first revenues from its Optical Circuit Switch product with two hyperscaler customers, a nascent line that management described as a long-run opportunity in AI fabric switching.

## Competitive Coordinates

Against Coherent Corp (COHR), the other principal listed Western supplier in 800G module hardware, the Lumentum competitive position operates at a different layer. Coherent assembles 800G modules; Lumentum sells those modules' EML chips. Hurlston acknowledged the dynamic without naming names:

> "Our components are embedded across the ecosystem, even in competitors' transceivers. That means we often win, regardless of who supplies the module." — *Q3 FY2025 earnings call*

Against the Marvell-Inphi axis — primarily DSP and co-packaged optics silicon — Lumentum's competition is largely orthogonal. Marvell's PAM4 DSP chips are used alongside Lumentum EMLs inside transceiver designs rather than instead of them.

## What the Dossier Asks

The Lumentum story entering fiscal 2026 rests on three open questions. First: how durable is hyperscaler AI capex in optical interconnect? Hurlston cited "greater than 25 percent compound annual growth rate over the next five years" for his addressable markets — a figure that depends on the continuing acceleration of AI cluster buildout at the five or six major cloud platforms. Second: can Lumentum defend the EML chokepoint as Coherent scales InP manufacturing, as Chinese merchant vendors (Innolight, Eoptolink) move up the component stack, and as co-packaged optics architectures eventually compress the pluggable module form factor? Third: what does Hurlston's strategic refocus actually deliver beyond the optical component market's cyclical tailwind — and does the Industrial Tech drag resolve? Each of those threads runs through the chapters that follow.

---

*Primary sources: [Lumentum IR press releases](https://investor.lumentum.com), [Q4 FY2025 earnings call transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/08/12/lumentum-lite-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/), [Q3 FY2025 earnings call transcript](https://www.stockinsights.ai/us/LITE/earnings-transcript/fy25-q3-d7f0), SEC EDGAR CIK 0001633978.*

chapters.title: From the August 2015 JDSU spin through Oclaro, NeoPhotonics, and Hurlston
chapters.body:
## The JDSU Spin-Off and the Standalone Lumentum

When JDS Uniphase completed the separation of its optical communications and commercial lasers businesses on August 1, 2015, it severed a corporate lineage that traced back through the fibre-optic boom and subsequent wreckage of the early 2000s. The resulting company — Lumentum Holdings, Inc., listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LITE — entered the market under Alan Lowe, a veteran of the old JDSU organisation who became its first president and chief executive officer. Headquartered in San Jose, California, Lumentum inherited a portfolio of optical communications components: transceivers, wavelength-selective switches, and the manufacturing infrastructure that had survived the telecom collapse. JDSU retained its network and service enablement division, later renamed Viavi Solutions. Lowe's initial mandate was structural — demonstrate that a focused merchant optical components company could generate consistent returns without the diversification drag of the parent.

The first full fiscal years as a standalone company — Lumentum's fiscal year runs to late June — produced revenues in the range of roughly $900 million to $1 billion. The business was grounded in telecom and datacom transceivers for equipment OEMs including Cisco, Nokia, and Ciena, alongside ROADMs that had become central to the long-haul and metropolitan network infrastructure being expanded by carriers. The commercial lasers segment — fibre lasers and solid-state lasers for industrial and semiconductor manufacturing applications — provided a secondary revenue base, serving customers including Trumpf, IPG Photonics, ASML, and Applied Materials. Lumentum was profitable but unremarkable in its early years; it was, to most analysts, a cyclical optical components play with a credible but limited addressable market.

## The Apple VCSEL Supercycle

The inflection came from an unexpected direction. When Apple introduced the iPhone X in September 2017 and embedded Face ID — a 3D facial-recognition system — in the device, it created demand for a specific class of optical component: the vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, or VCSEL. The Face ID module used an array of infrared-emitting VCSELs to project the structured-light pattern decoded for secure authentication. Apple's supply chain requirements were exacting and the volumes enormous. Lumentum became the principal VCSEL supplier for the programme, and the financial consequences were immediate.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue |
|---|---|
| FY2018 | $1.25 billion |
| FY2019 | $1.56 billion |
| FY2020 | $1.68 billion |
| FY2021 | $1.74 billion |
| FY2022 | $1.71 billion |
| FY2023 | $1.74 billion |
| FY2024 | $1.36 billion |

Revenue climbed from approximately $1.25 billion in fiscal 2018 to $1.56 billion in fiscal 2019 and $1.68 billion in fiscal 2020, driven substantially by Apple VCSEL volume. The 3D sensing product category that had not existed in Lumentum's original portfolio became its most visible growth lever. The concentration risk, however, was plain: a single consumer electronics customer with its own vertical-integration ambitions and the option to dual-source represented a structural vulnerability. Lowe's response was acquisition.

## The Oclaro Acquisition and Indium Phosphide Integration

In March 2018, Lumentum announced its intention to acquire Oclaro, Inc. — a San Jose-based optical components company with a critical asset: vertically integrated indium phosphide wafer fabrication. The transaction closed in December 2018 at an aggregate value of approximately $1.8 billion, a substantial premium for a company with roughly $600 million in annual revenue. [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978)

The strategic rationale was vertical integration at the chip level. Indium phosphide is the semiconductor substrate of choice for high-speed optical modulation at the wavelengths used in telecommunications and high-performance datacom links. Compound semiconductor fabrication at volume — InP wafers processed through clean-room facilities analogous to silicon fabs — was a capability that most optical component companies sourced externally from a small number of specialist foundries. Oclaro's InP fabrication facility in San Jose gave Lumentum direct control over the fundamental building block of its coherent transceiver products, reducing external dependency and, critically, providing a source of competitive advantage in a market where global InP capacity was structurally constrained.

The integration of Oclaro was operationally demanding. Lumentum absorbed a workforce of approximately 2,300 people across facilities in San Jose, Shenzhen, and elsewhere; the manufacturing rationalisation of two distinct fab environments required several years of execution. But the strategic architecture was sound: Lumentum emerged from the integration as one of the few vertically integrated merchant suppliers of indium phosphide-based optical components, able to offer telecom equipment OEMs and, increasingly, cloud infrastructure customers a level of supply chain security and technology depth that fabless competitors could not match.

## NeoPhotonics and the Coherent Technology Build-Out

The second major acquisition arrived three years later. In November 2021, Lumentum announced its agreement to acquire NeoPhotonics Corporation, a Santa Clara-based designer of coherent optical components and modules. Regulatory approval from Chinese authorities required until August 2022, when the transaction closed at approximately $918 million in cash. [investor.lumentum.com](https://investor.lumentum.com)

NeoPhotonics brought two strategic assets. First, a coherent transceiver technology platform — optical engines and narrow-linewidth lasers — that complemented Lumentum's existing wavelength-selective switch and ROADM product lines. Second, engineering talent: the NeoPhotonics team included deep expertise in the indium phosphide photonic integrated circuit architectures that coherent transmission at 400G and beyond required. Wupen Yuen, who had been a senior engineering leader at NeoPhotonics, joined Lumentum through the acquisition and became senior vice president for cloud-and-networking engineering.

The timing of the NeoPhotonics acquisition coincided with an emerging inflection in the datacom market: the transition from 400G to 800G transceiver standards driven by the hyperscaler community's investment in AI training and inference infrastructure. Dense GPU clusters interconnected at scale required optical transceivers capable of feeding petabits of data between compute nodes and the broader network fabric. The engineering depth that NeoPhotonics brought — narrow-linewidth laser sources, coherent DSP integration, photonic integration at InP — was directly applicable to the 800G and emerging 1.6T product generation that would define the cloud-and-datacenter revenue opportunity.

## Downturn, Succession, and the Hurlston Era

The period from mid-2023 through early 2024 was among the more difficult in Lumentum's history as a standalone company. The Apple VCSEL volume that had underpinned the revenue ramp from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2021 moderated as Apple diversified its VCSEL supply base and consumer 3D sensing volumes stabilised. Simultaneously, the broader telecommunications equipment market entered a sharp inventory correction as carriers reduced capital expenditure following years of elevated spending on 5G infrastructure and long-haul network expansion. Revenue in fiscal 2024 — the year ending late June 2024 — fell to approximately $1.36 billion, a compression of roughly $380 million from the $1.74 billion recorded in fiscal 2023.

Against that backdrop, the company announced a CEO transition in February 2024. Alan Lowe — who had led Lumentum since the August 2015 spin-off, a tenure of nearly nine years spanning the VCSEL supercycle, two major acquisitions, and the subsequent normalisation — stepped down. His successor was Michael Hurlston, who had most recently served as president and chief executive officer of Synaptics Incorporated from 2019 to 2024, and who before that had spent more than 19 years at Broadcom Limited in progressively senior roles, ultimately as senior vice president and general manager of the mobile connectivity products division.

Hurlston's appointment was calibrated to the moment. The Synaptics CEO tenure had required an analogous strategic refocus: taking a company known primarily for touchscreen controllers and redirecting it toward IoT and edge AI — a higher-growth, less commoditised product mix executed against a backdrop of rapid market transition. At Broadcom, Hurlston had managed high-volume, complex mixed-signal product lines through multiple semiconductor cycles. The combination — strategic-refocus experience plus high-volume execution discipline — was precisely what Lumentum's board was seeking as it positioned the company toward the 800G datacom opportunity.

Hurlston moved quickly to define the strategic priority. In communications accompanying his appointment, he framed Lumentum's indium phosphide vertical integration and coherent technology base — assembled across a decade and two acquisitions — as the competitive foundation for participation in the optical interconnect infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence workloads at scale. The cloud-and-datacenter category became the explicit centre of gravity: the organisation responsible for the 800G transceiver product ramp was led by Téa Williams as senior vice president for cloud and networking, with Yuen directing the engineering effort and the 1.6T transceiver generation positioned as the next product-cycle milestone.

Wajid Ali, who had served as executive vice president and chief financial officer since 2019, provided continuity across the CEO transition — a stability that allowed Hurlston to concentrate on strategic repositioning without the disruption of a simultaneous leadership change at the CFO function. Christopher Coldren, as senior vice president for strategy and corporate development, managed the ongoing NeoPhotonics integration and the broader framework for any further consolidation in a still-fragmented optical components industry.

The fiscal trajectory that followed the succession reflected the AI datacom inflection: cloud-and-datacenter revenues began recovering through fiscal 2025 as 800G transceiver volume at hyperscaler customers scaled, even as the telecom segment stabilised off its post-correction trough. The corporate architecture that emerged by mid-2025 — indium phosphide vertical integration, coherent transceiver depth, cloud-and-datacenter strategic focus, and a CEO with a mandate to execute the AI optical interconnect opportunity — reflected a decade of accumulation that had begun with a quiet spin-off on a summer day in 2015.

chapters.title: Optical Communications, Commercial Lasers, and the cloud-and-datacenter inflection
chapters.body:
## Two Businesses, One Inflection Point

Lumentum Holdings entered the world as a listed company in August 2015, carved out from the ruins of JDS Uniphase in a demerger that separated optical components from the network test-and-measurement equipment that JDSU's other half — the entity that would become Viavi Solutions — would retain. The optics business Lumentum inherited was a formidable one: deep manufacturing expertise in indium phosphide laser chips, a substantial position in reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers for telecom carriers, and a growing relationship with Apple Inc., whose Face ID biometric system had begun to consume Lumentum's vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser arrays at a rate that, by the early 2020s, accounted for roughly a quarter of group revenues in peak years.

That consumer dependency defined the company's middle period — rewarding but volatile, ultimately bounded by the upgrade cadence of a single handset platform. When Michael Hurlston succeeded founder chief executive Alan Lowe in February 2024, he inherited a business that had already begun the shift away from that dependency — and an optical components franchise that was simultaneously the largest merchant supplier of electroabsorption modulated lasers for the datacentre interconnect market in the world. The question he faced was how quickly the hyperscale buildout could absorb Lumentum's expanding capacity, and how decisively the company could redirect its engineering priorities toward the cloud.

Lumentum reports across two segments. What was called Optical Communications — the dominant franchise, encompassing transceivers, coherent components, indium phosphide chips and ROADMs — was renamed Cloud & Networking beginning in the first quarter of fiscal 2024, signalling the strategic priority shift explicitly. Commercial Lasers, the smaller and slower-growing segment serving industrial materials-processing, semiconductor equipment, and scientific applications, was simultaneously relabelled Industrial Tech.

## The Revenue Record: Trough, Recovery, Inflection

The fiscal year ending June 2024 represented the cyclical nadir. Total revenue fell to $1.36bn, down 23% from $1.77bn in fiscal 2023, as the double blow of Apple VCSEL normalisation and a severe telecom equipment-spending downturn compressed both segments simultaneously. Cloud & Networking — the larger segment — fell to $1.08bn; Industrial Tech to $274m, a decline of 38% year on year reflecting the collapse in imaging and sensing product demand tied to the consumer electronics cycle.

| Fiscal Year (ending June) | Cloud & Networking | Industrial Tech | Total Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $1,519m | $194m | $1,713m |
| FY2023 | $1,558m | $209m | $1,767m |
| FY2024 | $1,085m | $274m | $1,359m |
| FY2025 | $1,411m | $234m | $1,645m |

The recovery through fiscal 2025 was driven almost entirely by the Cloud & Networking segment, which expanded 30% as 800G transceiver volumes began their compound ascent at hyperscaler data centres. Industrial Tech, by contrast, contracted a further 15% in fiscal 2025, weighed by continued declines in imaging and sensing revenue. The divergence between segments — photonics for AI infrastructure accelerating, photonics for consumer and light industrial applications declining — had by fiscal 2025 become the central financial story of the company. [SEC EDGAR FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/0001628280-25-040830-index.htm)

Quarterly momentum into the second half of fiscal 2025 and the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 was sharper still. The quarter ending June 2025 produced $481m in group revenue, rising to $534m in the September 2025 quarter, $666m in December 2025, and $808m — a 90% year-on-year gain — in the quarter ending March 2026. [Q3 FY2026 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001633978/000162828026030530/lite_ex991xq3fy26.htm)

## Optical Communications: EML Chips and the 800G Architecture

The engine of the Cloud & Networking segment is Lumentum's electroabsorption modulated laser franchise. EML chips — the semiconductor devices that modulate optical signals in high-speed data links — are the critical active component in 800G transceivers, the standard interconnect format deployed across hyperscale AI data centres through 2024 and 2025. Industry analysts estimated that Lumentum supplied approximately half of world EML volume, a position underwritten by indium phosphide fabrication capacity that few merchant suppliers could replicate at comparable scale.

The 100G-per-lane EML, the building block of 800G transceiver assemblies, was the primary revenue driver through the period. Hurlston reported that EML shipments achieved an all-time record in the quarter ending June 2025, with revenue "nearly doubling" relative to the baseline of twelve months earlier. By the March 2026 quarter, the higher-specification 200G-per-lane EML — the component required for 1.6T transceiver architectures — had become material, with its revenues rising 128% sequentially in a single quarter as early qualification programmes at hyperscaler customers converted into initial production volumes. [Q3 FY2026 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001633978/000162828026030530/lite_ex991xq3fy26.htm)

Lumentum further extended its position in the transceiver supply chain through the November 2023 acquisition of Cloud Light, a module assembly business, at a cost of approximately $750m. Where the company had historically sold laser chips to transceiver assemblers, Cloud Light's integration enabled Lumentum to package its own EML and continuous-wave laser chips into finished transceiver modules sold directly to hyperscaler procurement teams. By the quarter ending June 2025, Hurlston confirmed that modules were shipping to "all three of our major hyperscale customers."

The coherent transceiver layer — used for longer-haul and data centre interconnect applications — was reinforced by the August 2022 acquisition of NeoPhotonics at approximately $918m. [SEC EDGAR 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978) NeoPhotonics brought tunable laser and photonic integrated circuit technology for high-baud-rate coherent systems; the integration was declared complete within the first fiscal year, with operating expense synergies exceeding the initial $20m annual target. By 2025, NeoPhotonics-derived coherent component technology underpinned Lumentum's position in the ZR and ZR+ coherent pluggable formats, which Wupen Yuen, the company's president of Cloud & Networking, described as representing a structural shift in hyperscaler networking:

> "ZR market is growing very rapidly. There's a very general trend now for most of the hyperscalers to resort to the ZR kind of architecture, moving away from traditional transponder-based architectures."

ROADMs — reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers deployed by telecom carriers — remained the other principal sub-segment within Cloud & Networking. Telecom demand had been severely depressed through fiscal 2024, as carriers digested excess inventory accumulated during the post-pandemic equipment cycle. The telecom recovery lagged the datacom inflection by several quarters and, as of early 2026, supply constraints in indium phosphide wafer capacity were prioritising datacom over telecom output.

## Commercial Lasers: Industrial Durability, Consumer Retreat

The Industrial Tech segment — legacy Commercial Lasers — occupied a structurally different position. Its revenue base comprised industrial fibre lasers and beam-delivery systems used in metal cutting, welding, and additive manufacturing; specialised solid-state and CO₂ lasers for semiconductor lithography support (including EUV-adjacent equipment supplied to the ASML ecosystem); and the residual 3D sensing VCSEL business tied to Apple's Face ID platform.

The Apple relationship had defined the segment's peak years. At the height of iPhone VCSEL volumes in fiscal 2020 and 2021, the consumer sensing business accounted for roughly a quarter of total group revenue. The company subsequently disclosed that its expectation for the consumer customer was "less than 10% of annual revenue going forward, absent a favourable product or technology shift." By fiscal 2024, Apple had ceased to appear among the customers individually representing more than 10% of revenue in Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

Industrial Tech revenue fell from $274m in fiscal 2024 to $234m in fiscal 2025 — a further 15% decline, attributed to lower imaging and sensing product sales and the ongoing moderation of consumer legacy volumes. Gross margins in the segment were also compressed by the shift in mix away from higher-margin sensing products. Against the extraordinary acceleration in Cloud & Networking, Industrial Tech had become a cash-generative but secondary contributor: approximately 14% of group revenue in fiscal 2025, declining in absolute terms as the cloud-and-datacenter franchise scaled.

The long-term strategic rationale for retaining the Industrial Tech segment rested on its laser technology synergies — InP and solid-state laser manufacturing know-how feeds both the industrial product line and the datacom chip portfolio — and on the semiconductor equipment exposure, which provided some leverage on capital expenditure cycles in advanced logic and memory fabrication.

## Cloud and Datacenter: Hyperscaler Concentration and the 800G Ramp

Customer concentration deepened substantially as the cloud inflection gathered velocity. The fiscal 2025 annual report, filed with the SEC in August 2025, disclosed that two unnamed customers each individually exceeded 10% of total net revenue: one at 16.0% and one at 15.4% of the fiscal year total. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/0001628280-25-040830-index.htm) Management commentary on earnings calls made clear that the customers driving the majority of transceiver volume were hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure operators. Hurlston characterised the ordering dynamic with unusual directness on the fiscal first-quarter 2026 call:

> "Pretty much the majority of all of this is coming from our largest customer."

He had earlier articulated the strategic decision to concentrate supply deliberately:

> "We do not expect to add customers beyond these three for the next several quarters."

The supply side was simultaneously the binding constraint and the strategic moat. Lumentum's indium phosphide fabrication infrastructure — anchored in facilities in Sagamihara and Takao in Japan and Caswell in the United Kingdom, inherited principally from the December 2018 Oclaro acquisition at approximately $1.8bn — was described by management as "fully subscribed to at least the end of calendar 2025" as of fiscal 2024. Capital expenditure in fiscal 2025 reached $231m as the company executed a 40% expansion in InP wafer capacity, with further 40% expansion committed for fiscal 2026. The transition to 6-inch InP wafer substrates, which Yuen described as providing "a few times of the capacity over the next several years," was underway as of the review period.

The broader strategic significance of the InP position was acknowledged by Nvidia Corporation in March 2026, when the chip designer invested $2.0bn in Lumentum through a private placement of Series A convertible preferred stock at $695.31 per share. The investment was accompanied by a multi-billion-dollar non-exclusive purchase commitment and co-development arrangements for co-packaged optics and silicon photonics targeting what Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang described as "gigawatt-scale AI factories." [NVIDIA Newsroom, March 2026](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-announces-strategic-partnership-with-lumentum-to-develop-state-of-the-art-optics-technology)

## 1.6T and the Next Architecture Cycle

The transition from 800G to 1.6T transceiver architectures — each doubling per-port bandwidth by moving from 100G-per-lane to 200G-per-lane EML technology — was still in its early stages at the frozen snapshot date of May 2026. Yuen characterised the hyperscaler installed base as predominantly still on the 800G platform "for probably the next couple of years at a minimum," even as qualification activity on 1.6T transceivers had begun converting to initial production orders. Hurlston indicated that Lumentum had line of sight to shipping 1.6T transceivers into volume production "sometime middle-ish" of calendar 2026.

The financial logic of the generational transition was favourable. Chief financial officer Wajid Ali indicated that gross margins on 1.6T products were expected to be "significantly better than 800G margins" — a function of higher average selling prices for 200G EML chips, relative to the cost structure already established in InP fabrication. The 200G EML's share of data centre laser chip revenue was approximately 10% of the mix in early 2026, rising rapidly as qualification programmes completed.

The optical circuit switch — a photonic switching product enabling software-defined routing of optical signals within data centre fabrics — represented an adjacent growth lever that Lumentum was scaling in parallel. The OCS order book exceeded $400m by the first quarter of fiscal 2026, with two hyperscalers in volume deployment and a third committed for calendar 2026. Hurlston set a public target of $100m per quarter in OCS revenue by December 2026. Co-packaged optics — the integration of laser and photonic components directly onto switch packages — constituted a further horizon that management described as entering its initial ramp phase, with volume production targeted for the second half of calendar 2026.

> "As our key growth drivers of co-packaged optics and optical circuit switches begin to kick in, we would expect further increases in earnings power." — Michael Hurlston, March 2026 earnings call.

The trajectory from the August 2015 JDSU spin — through the Apple dependency, the Oclaro vertical integration, the NeoPhotonics coherent layer, and the Cloud Light module assembly entry — had by the spring of 2026 converged on a single dominant narrative: Lumentum as the principal listed merchant supplier of the photonic infrastructure underpinning the AI data centre buildout. The two segments that structured its financial reporting told that story in inverse: one accelerating at a rate the company's supply infrastructure was straining to match; the other generating cash against a gradually receding revenue base, waiting for the next consumer or industrial technology cycle to renew it.

chapters.title: FY2024 $1.36B trough, FY2025 recovery, and the cloud-and-datacenter mix shift
chapters.body:
## The anatomy of a trough

Revenue had climbed steadily from $1.25 billion in fiscal 2018 — the first full year as an independent company following the August 2015 JDS Uniphase spin-off — to a plateau around $1.74 billion that persisted across fiscal years 2021, 2022, and 2023. Then, in fiscal 2024, the twelve months ended late June 2024, Lumentum recorded net revenue of approximately $1.36 billion: a compression of roughly 22 percent from the plateau and the lowest annual reading since the years immediately following the JDSU separation.

Two forces converged to produce that trough. The first was the familiar cyclicality of the telecom components industry: after a multi-year spend cycle by network operators and their equipment OEM intermediaries — Cisco, Nokia, Ericsson, Ciena, Infinera — demand collapsed in 2023 as inventory accumulated at every node along the optical networking supply chain. The second was structural. Lumentum's largest single-product revenue contributor for much of the prior cycle had been vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers consumed by Apple's 3D-sensing Face ID modules. As Apple diversified its VCSEL sourcing and the underlying design cycle matured, that revenue stream moderated, removing a high-margin cushion that had supported the consolidated gross margin profile through fiscal 2019 and 2020.

## Revenue trajectory: FY2018–FY2024

| Fiscal Year | Net Revenue | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|
| FY2018 | $1.25B | — |
| FY2019 | $1.56B | +25% |
| FY2020 | $1.68B | +8% |
| FY2021 | $1.74B | +4% |
| FY2022 | $1.71B | −2% |
| FY2023 | $1.74B | +2% |
| FY2024 | $1.36B | −22% |

*Sources: Lumentum annual reports filed with [SEC EDGAR, CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978); [investor.lumentum.com](https://investor.lumentum.com)*

The fiscal 2019 surge from $1.25 billion to $1.56 billion reflected the first full-cycle contribution of the 3D sensing franchise alongside telecom spending strength. The Oclaro acquisition, which closed in December 2018 for approximately $1.8 billion in Lumentum stock, brought indium phosphide chip fabrication at San Jose and Shenzhen into the corporate perimeter and widened the optical communications revenue base heading into fiscal 2020. Revenue continued to grow modestly through fiscal 2021 despite pandemic-era supply disruption, as network operators accelerated optical capacity investment and the 3D sensing line remained productive.

The fiscal 2022–2023 plateau at approximately $1.71–1.74 billion was, in retrospect, deceptive. Within that flat headline, the mix was quietly shifting: telecom remained the dominant contributor, Apple 3D sensing was declining as a share of the total, and the nascent cloud-and-datacenter category — principally 100G and early 400G transceivers for hyperscaler customers — was growing but had not yet reached the scale needed to offset the structural telecom concentration. The NeoPhotonics acquisition, which closed in August 2022 at approximately $918 million in cash, added coherent transceiver intellectual property and further indium phosphide process capability; it also added purchase-price amortisation and integration costs at a moment when the telecom cycle was approaching its peak.

## Gross margin compression and the cost of underutilisation

The revenue decline in fiscal 2024 inflicted asymmetric damage on margins. Optical components manufacturing is capital-intensive and heavily fixed-cost: Lumentum operates indium phosphide and gallium arsenide fabrication facilities in San Jose, Ottawa, Shenzhen, and Bangkok. When volume falls sharply, unabsorbed factory overhead flows directly through the income statement.

Lumentum's GAAP gross margin was materially compressed in fiscal 2024, reflecting three concurrent drags. First, volume deleverage across the telecom product lines — reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers, coherent transmission modules, and merchant optical components for OEM customers — left fabrication capacity running well below historical utilisation levels. Second, inventory write-downs flowed through cost of revenue as the telecom channel absorbed excess components that had been ordered during the spending cycle. Third, the accumulated amortisation of acquired intangibles from both the Oclaro and NeoPhotonics transactions continued to weigh on reported gross profit at a moment when the underlying operating leverage had turned sharply negative.

Non-GAAP gross margins, which exclude intangible amortisation and stock-based compensation and are the basis on which Lumentum typically guided investors, told a somewhat less severe story — but even on that adjusted basis, the magnitude of volume deleverage through the fiscal 2024 quarters was visible in sequential compression. The company's two-segment structure provided limited shelter: Commercial Lasers, serving industrial fabrication customers such as Trumpf and IPG Photonics and semiconductor equipment OEMs including ASML and Applied Materials, carried its own cyclicality tied to semiconductor capital expenditure and was itself navigating softer demand through the same period.

## Capital structure and the convertible debt burden

The twin acquisition programme — Oclaro in December 2018 and NeoPhotonics in August 2022 — left Lumentum with a capital structure shaped by both the equity issued for Oclaro and the cash deployed for NeoPhotonics. In connection with the NeoPhotonics financing and broader balance-sheet management, Lumentum carried approximately $575 million of 0.50% Convertible Senior Notes due December 2026, an instrument issued during the low-interest-rate environment that preceded the Federal Reserve's 2022 tightening cycle and structured to provide low-cost capital while limiting near-term cash interest expense. [SEC EDGAR, CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978)

Those notes, convertible into Lumentum common stock at a fixed premium to the prevailing share price at issuance, created a maturity management obligation that the company — and fixed-income investors — would need to navigate as it emerged from the revenue trough. The December 2026 maturity sat close enough on the horizon to be a visible overhang on investor sentiment during fiscal 2024, particularly as the share price had retreated materially from the levels prevailing when the notes were issued, reducing the likelihood of conversion and increasing the probability of cash repayment or refinancing at higher prevailing rates.

The balance sheet did carry meaningful liquidity: Lumentum had historically maintained a cash and short-term investment position in the $1.0–1.5 billion range through the acquisition cycle, and the company entered the fiscal 2024 downturn from a position of operational solvency rather than financial distress. Nevertheless, the combination of the approaching convertible maturity, weak operating cash generation during the trough, and a share price that had declined from its cycle peak materially narrowed the financial flexibility that had characterised the company's posture in the peak years.

## Hurlston's succession and the strategic reframe

In February 2024, midway through the fiscal year, Michael Hurlston succeeded Alan Lowe as chief executive. Lowe had built Lumentum as an independent company from the JDSU spin and had executed both the Oclaro and NeoPhotonics acquisitions, but the combination of the telecom market collapse and the 3D sensing revenue decline had left the company in a strategic void, with two large and partially-integrated acquisitions whose revenue contributions were being tested by the same cyclical and structural forces that had motivated them.

Hurlston arrived from Synaptics, where he had managed a portfolio reorientation from commodity fingerprint sensing toward higher-value connectivity and display technology — a playbook with structural parallels to Lumentum's situation. Before Synaptics, he had run mobile connectivity at Broadcom, a background that positioned him to engage credibly with hyperscaler procurement teams navigating the 800G optical interconnect buildout for artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The cloud-and-datacenter thesis was not structurally new at Lumentum: the optical communications segment had supplied 100G and 400G transceiver components to cloud customers for years. What changed under Hurlston was emphasis and capital-allocation signalling. The cloud-and-datacenter category — 800G transceivers for AI training and inference cluster interconnect, and the emerging 1.6T generation on the product roadmap — was reframed as the principal forward growth driver, with telecom repositioned as a stable but cyclical counterweight rather than the strategic centre of mass.

## The 800G inflection and cloud-and-datacenter mix shift

The mechanics of the mix shift matter because they bear directly on the margin recovery path. Datacom transceivers for the 800G generation — modules destined for AI cluster switch fabrics and front-end-of-rack interconnects at hyperscaler data centres — carry different revenue and margin characteristics than the telecom ROADMs and coherent line-side modules that had historically anchored the optical communications segment.

At 800G, module architecture centred on combinations of directly-modulated lasers and electro-absorption modulated lasers, technologies in which Lumentum's indium phosphide fabrication facilities had accumulated years of process learning originating with the Oclaro acquisition. The vertical integration meant that margin capture extended from the chip layer through component assembly, rather than being shared with an external InP foundry — a structural advantage that was becoming more commercially relevant as the merchant InP foundry market remained capacity-constrained relative to the scale of hyperscaler demand.

As 800G volume ramped at hyperscaler customers through fiscal 2024 and into fiscal 2025, improving factory utilisation at the indium phosphide facilities began to offset the continued softness in telecom, gradually shifting the gross margin profile back toward more normalised levels. The NeoPhotonics IP, meanwhile, contributed to coherent transceiver roadmap credibility as early signs of telecom inventory normalisation began to emerge.

| Revenue Driver | FY2024 Character | Direction entering FY2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud & Datacenter (800G) | Growing but not yet offsetting telecom | Principal growth engine |
| Telecom ROADMs & coherent | Sharp cyclical decline; inventory digestion | Stabilising; early recovery |
| Apple 3D sensing VCSELs | Structural moderation, diminished share | Persistent but reduced |
| Commercial Lasers | Semiconductor equipment softness | Recovering with capex cycle |

*Sources: [Lumentum investor relations](https://investor.lumentum.com); [SEC EDGAR, CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978)*

The arc from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2024 — $1.25 billion, a $1.74 billion peak, and a $1.36 billion trough — traced the complete cycle of a components company navigating acquisition-driven transformation, end-market cyclicality, and a structural pivot toward cloud infrastructure. The Oclaro deal had purchased the manufacturing foundation: indium phosphide vertical integration that no amount of fabless design capability could replicate quickly. The NeoPhotonics deal had layered coherent capacity on top at a cost that looked elevated at the 2022 closing and looked strategically defensible by 2024. What the fiscal 2024 trough clarified, with the unambiguous logic of a down-cycle income statement, was that the returns on both acquisitions would be realised not in telecom's next up-cycle alone, but through the convergence of hyperscaler 800G demand with Lumentum's uniquely integrated indium phosphide supply chain — the bet that Hurlston inherited, and chose to press.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Multiple in Context

As of the frozen snapshot date — 23 May 2026 — Lumentum Holdings trades under the ticker **LITE** on the NASDAQ. Precise closing-price data is not pinned in the primary-source record available to this dossier; the analysis below reasons explicitly from the last-reported diluted share count (approximately 66–68 million shares, as disclosed in Lumentum's most recent 10-K and 10-Q filings with the SEC under [CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978)) and the price range that has characterised the stock over the preceding twelve months, which oscillated broadly between approximately $60 and $95. Using a midpoint assumption of roughly **$75 per share** yields an equity market capitalisation of approximately **$5.0–5.1 billion**. With net debt estimated at approximately $1.1–1.3 billion — the residual load from the $1.8 billion Oclaro acquisition and the $918 million NeoPhotonics deal, partially absorbed by cash generation as 800G transceiver revenues inflected — the implied enterprise value sits in the band of **$6.1–6.4 billion**. All multiples below are computed from this range and from financial data disclosed in Lumentum's [SEC filings](https://investor.lumentum.com/financial-information/sec-filings).

## Current Multiples

The fundamental challenge in applying conventional multiples to Lumentum at this juncture is the depth of the trough from which the business is recovering. Fiscal 2024 revenue — the year ending late June 2024 — landed at approximately **$1.36 billion**, compressed sharply from the $1.71–1.74 billion plateau of fiscal 2021–2023 by the simultaneous unwinding of Apple VCSEL volumes and the 2023–2024 telecom inventory correction. That trough year produced operating losses and EBITDA that was negligible or negative, making trailing earnings-based multiples misleading rather than informative.

The forward frame is more instructive:

| Multiple | Basis | Estimated Range |
|---|---|---|
| EV/Sales (trailing FY2024) | $1.36B revenue | 4.5–4.7× |
| EV/Sales (forward FY2025E) | ~$1.7–1.9B estimate | 3.2–3.8× |
| Forward P/E (FY2025E) | ~$1.50–$2.50 EPS estimate | 30–50× |
| EV/EBITDA (forward FY2025E) | ~$200–$300M EBITDA estimate | 20–30× |
| Price/Book | Tangible book negative; total book ~$2.5B | ~2.0× |

*FY2025 estimates are derived from management guidance trajectories and consensus ranges visible through Q3 FY2025 earnings disclosures. Exact fiscal 2025 full-year results may not yet be reported as of the frozen snapshot.*

The forward EV/Sales range of 3–4× reflects the market's willingness to pay well above a melting-ice-cube industrial multiple — typically 1–2× for a structurally declining hardware franchise — for a business that sits at the centre of the AI-driven optical interconnect build-out. The wide forward P/E band reflects genuine uncertainty about whether Lumentum can convert 800G revenue growth into durable net income, given the cost burden of carrying two dilutive acquisitions and a commercial-lasers segment that has run below corporate cost-of-capital returns for several years.

## Historical Context: Re-rating and De-rating

From the August 2015 JDSU spin through the peak of the Apple VCSEL supercycle — roughly fiscal 2019–2021 — LITE traded at optically rich multiples: EV/Sales of 4–6× and forward P/Es of 25–35×, on the narrative that indium phosphide chip-to-module integration gave the company structural pricing power and captive customer uplift. The $1.8 billion Oclaro acquisition in December 2018 added revenue but also brought an estimated $1.5 billion in goodwill and intangibles that compressed return on invested capital and became a persistent drag on book value.

The subsequent de-rating was severe. By the fiscal 2024 trough, the stock had shed roughly 60–70 percent from its 2021 highs, compressing EV/Sales toward 2.5–3.0× at the late-2023 lows and pushing trailing EBITDA multiples into negative territory. The pattern is characteristic of semiconductor and optical cycles — peak-multiple narrative stocks mean-revert on EBITDA in the down-leg — but the speed of the reset was amplified by the Apple volume normalisation and the telecom digestion cycle landing simultaneously rather than sequentially.

The partial recovery into the 2024–2025 AI datacom tailwind represents a selective re-rating: EV/Sales has expanded from the trough back toward 3.5–4.5×, but the stock has not reclaimed prior peak multiples, reflecting residual uncertainty about margin trajectory and the pace of the 1.6T upgrade cycle.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The optical components peer group spans a wide range of business models — from pure-play transceiver manufacturers to vertically integrated chip-and-module platforms to contract photonic assemblers. The table below places Lumentum against its most relevant publicly traded comparators.

| Company | Ticker | EV/Sales (fwd) | EV/EBITDA (fwd) | Fwd P/E | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lumentum Holdings | LITE | 3.2–3.8× | 20–30× | 30–50× | InP-vertical integration; 800G ramp; trough recovery |
| Coherent Corp | COHR | 2.8–3.5× | 18–25× | 25–40× | Broadest optical portfolio; II-VI integration still digesting |
| Ciena Corporation | CIEN | 2.5–3.0× | 15–20× | 22–30× | Networking-layer optical; less chip-level IP |
| Fabrinet | FN | 1.8–2.5× | 14–18× | 22–28× | Contract manufacturing premium; lower IP value |
| Applied Optoelectronics | AAOI | 3.5–5.0× | NM–25× | NM–35× | Smaller, higher 800G growth leverage; volatile |
| Viavi Solutions | VIAV | 1.5–2.0× | 10–14× | 14–20× | Test and measurement mix; limited AI-datacom exposure |

Lumentum trades at a modest premium to Coherent on EV/Sales, reflecting credit for InP integration and the relative purity of its AI-datacom exposure versus Coherent's broader franchise. The premium to Fabrinet and Viavi is structurally supported by the chip-to-module vertical, which generates IP-driven pricing power unavailable to a contract assembler. The discount to Applied Optoelectronics on EV/Sales reflects size, liquidity, and the scarcity premium markets assign to high-growth small-caps in a hot cycle.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Price Implies

A simplified reverse-engineering of the $6.1–6.4 billion enterprise value against a five-year discounted-cash-flow framework is instructive as a discipline check. Assuming a weighted-average cost of capital of approximately 10–11% — consistent with a moderately levered optical-components company carrying semiconductor-like cyclicality — and a terminal-growth rate of 3–4%, the current EV implies the market expects Lumentum to generate **normalised free cash flow of roughly $350–450 million per annum** within the five-year forecast window, approximately fiscal 2028–2030.

That requires a free-cash-flow margin of approximately 18–22% on revenues of $1.9–2.3 billion. This is materially above fiscal 2024 operating margins but broadly consistent with the margin profile the business demonstrated at peak operating leverage in fiscal 2019–2021, before the NeoPhotonics integration costs and the volume deleverage of the telecom correction compressed results. The implied scenario is therefore neither heroic nor trivial: it prices in a successful 800G and emerging 1.6T revenue ramp, restoration of gross margins toward the 40–45% corridor, and meaningful operating-leverage recovery from the cost discipline Michael Hurlston has imposed since taking the chief-executive seat in February 2024.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $120–140 per share:** The AI hyperscaler optical build-out sustains multi-year compound growth in the cloud-and-datacenter segment. 800G average-selling-price declines are offset by volume expansion, and an accelerating 1.6T upgrade cycle opens fresh revenue pools in the fiscal 2027–2028 window. Lumentum's InP manufacturing scale becomes a supply constraint that competitors cannot close within three to four years, enabling gross margins to recover toward 48–50%. Revenue reaches $2.3–2.5 billion by fiscal 2027, EBITDA margins normalise to 25–28%, and the stock re-rates toward 5× forward EV/Sales and 22–25× forward EBITDA — a premium warranted by the scarcity of comparable vertically integrated assets. This scenario requires no material hyperscaler capital-expenditure pause, no InP capacity announcement from a captive hyperscaler optical programme, and successful execution of the NeoPhotonics coherent platform in the carrier market.

**Base case — $70–90 per share:** 800G volumes ramp broadly in line with guidance, the telecom segment stabilises at approximately $400–450 million annually without a meaningful cyclical recovery, and Lumentum compounds cloud-and-datacenter revenue at 20–25% through fiscal 2026–2027 before growth moderates toward the high-single digits. Gross margins recover to 42–45% by fiscal 2026 on volume absorption, and operating margins return to the low-to-mid teens. Revenue reaches $1.9–2.1 billion by fiscal 2027. The multiple stays in the 3.5–4.5× EV/Sales corridor, and the stock drifts modestly higher absent a significant earnings acceleration or forward-guidance revision. This is the scenario the market appears, on balance, to be pricing.

**Bear case — $40–55 per share:** Hyperscaler AI infrastructure investment cycles down after the 2024–2025 surge — a risk visible in historical capex digestion patterns — 800G pricing compresses faster than volume grows, and a second telecom inventory correction in 2026–2027 coincides with the datacom deceleration. The NeoPhotonics integration underperforms; the coherent-platform revenue trajectory disappoints on a multi-year view, a risk that remains live given the complexity of absorbing two acquisitions valued at over $2.7 billion in under four years. Revenue plateaus at $1.5–1.7 billion, EBITDA margins remain in the high-single-digit to low-double-digit range, and the enterprise value returns toward trough levels. In this scenario, balance-sheet leverage from acquisition debt becomes a more material refinancing and financial-flexibility concern.

## What the Market Is Pricing — and the Gap

Consensus appears to be broadly pricing the base case: a controlled 800G ramp, gradual margin recovery, and a stock that drifts moderately higher through fiscal 2026 as quarterly earnings prove achievable. What consensus does not appear to fully price is the structural supply-side advantage Lumentum holds through InP vertical integration on a three-to-five-year horizon, nor the strategic optionality embedded in the NeoPhotonics coherent platform should carrier spend recover meaningfully into fiscal 2027.

The dossier's read leans marginally constructive relative to consensus. The InP manufacturing advantage is durable in a way that is difficult to value from the outside — it represents decades of process investment and the absorption of essentially all available merchant InP capacity following the Oclaro acquisition. The Hurlston-era operating discipline, visible in leaner headcount and the explicit reorientation of capital allocation toward cloud-and-datacenter margin targets, has the hallmarks of management that has correctly identified where the franchise value accrues. The principal risk the dossier weights above the market is execution risk on the NeoPhotonics integration: two acquisitions in four years, both at premium valuations, leave limited margin for error if the coherent platform's revenue trajectory disappoints. The stock is not cheap on trailing metrics, not obviously expensive on forward multiples if the cycle delivers, and carries the classic photonics-sector tension between secular bandwidth demand and cyclical amplification that has repeatedly wrong-footed both bulls and bears in this space.

chapters.title: Post-Hurlston quarters and the cloud-and-datacenter trajectory
chapters.body:
## From trough to inflection: Lowe's final chapters set the table

When Alan Lowe reported third-quarter fiscal 2024 results in May of that year, Lumentum was navigating what had become a painful double compression. The fiscal year that would close in June 2024 was on track to produce roughly $1.36 billion in revenue — down nearly a quarter from the $1.77 billion recorded in fiscal 2023 — as a post-Apple VCSEL normalisation collided with a generalised telecom spending freeze. Yet beneath the headline pressure, a different story was quietly assembling itself.

Cloud and Networking revenue for the March 2024 quarter reached $313.8 million, representing 85.6 percent of the company's $366.5 million total. Datacom laser chip orders had reached record levels, anchored by electroabsorption-modulated laser, or EML, chips used in high-speed transceiver modules destined for hyperscaler data centres. The non-GAAP gross margin held at 32.6 percent — constrained, but stable. Lowe told investors that data-centre revenues had achieved a record quarter, and that the company was investing in additional production capacity in Thailand to meet what it described as allocation-level demand.

The fourth quarter of fiscal 2024, closed June 2024, was messier: Cloud and Networking revenue fell 18.8 percent sequentially to $254.7 million, partly reflecting customer ordering patterns rather than demand erosion, and full-year revenue settled at $1.359 billion. But even in the trough, Lowe flagged record datacom chip orders and warned that InP laser capacity would remain on allocation through at least the end of calendar 2025. The implication for the investor class was plain: the supply side, not the demand side, was the binding constraint.

## Three hyperscalers and the EML record-book

The fiscal 2025 ramp began in the September 2024 quarter. Cloud and Networking revenue recovered to $282.3 million and then, in the December quarter, surged 20.2 percent sequentially to $339.2 million — the first unmistakable sign that the 800-gigabit per second wave was arriving in volume. Lumentum set another EML shipment record, including new 200-gigabit lane-speed variants. Management disclosed it had begun ramping cloud transceiver volumes to its largest hyperscaler customer and a second new customer, and by November 2024 had confirmed a third hyperscale qualification, with initial volume production expected in the first half of calendar 2025.

| Quarter | Revenue | Non-GAAP GM% | Cloud & Networking / Components |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 FY2024 (Mar 2024) | $366.5M | 32.6% | $313.8M |
| Q4 FY2024 (Jun 2024) | $308.3M | 32.2% | $254.7M |
| Q1 FY2025 (Sep 2024) | $336.9M | 32.8% | $282.3M |
| Q2 FY2025 (Dec 2024) | $402.2M | 32.3% | $339.2M |
| Q3 FY2025 (Mar 2025) | $425.2M | 35.2% | $365.2M |
| Q4 FY2025 (Jun 2025) | $480.7M | 37.8% | $424.1M |
| Q1 FY2026 (Sep 2025) | $533.8M | 39.4% | $379.2M |
| Q2 FY2026 (Dec 2025) | $665.5M | 42.5% | $444.0M |
| Q3 FY2026 (Mar 2026) | $808.4M | 47.9% | $533.0M |

On 3 February 2025 — the same day Lumentum released preliminary second-quarter fiscal 2025 results showing $402.2 million in revenue and a non-GAAP operating margin of 7.9 percent — the company announced that Michael Hurlston would succeed Lowe as President and Chief Executive Officer, effective 7 February. The timing was deliberate: Lumentum wanted the earnings cadence and the leadership transition to be read together. The company Hurlston was inheriting was already accelerating.

## Hurlston's first ninety days

Hurlston took the earnings-call podium for the first time on 6 May 2025, reporting the March-quarter results. Revenue for the quarter ended 29 March 2025 reached $425.2 million, beating the high end of guidance, with Cloud and Networking at $365.2 million — up 16.4 percent year-over-year. The non-GAAP gross margin expanded 290 basis points sequentially to 35.2 percent, and the non-GAAP operating margin reached 10.8 percent.

His opening remarks set the register he would maintain throughout the subsequent quarters:

> "In my first 90 days as CEO, it's become clear that Lumentum is uniquely positioned to lead as the convergence of optics and electronics accelerates AI data center scaling. Our innovations — from advanced EMLs to ultra-high-power lasers — are driving transformative power efficiencies across cloud, AI, and long-haul networks, making us an essential partner in this next era of connectivity."

Hurlston also announced the R300 optical circuit switch for AI cluster and data-centre network applications — a product line that would prove disproportionately significant over the following four quarters. He set a public target: $500 million in quarterly revenue by the end of calendar 2025.

## The compound acceleration

The June 2025 quarter delivered $480.7 million in revenue against original guidance of $440 to $470 million — Lumentum had in fact raised its outlook mid-quarter via an 8-K filing before beating even the revised range. The non-GAAP gross margin reached 37.8 percent, up 260 basis points sequentially and fully 1,000 basis points above the year-prior reading. Cloud and Networking revenue climbed to $424.1 million, a 67 percent year-over-year advance. EML shipments reached an all-time high. Lumentum received what Hurlston described as the largest single co-packaged optics laser purchase commitment in the company's history. The optical circuit switch business recognised its first revenue, shipping to two customers.

On capacity constraints Hurlston was candid:

> "We're honestly limited by capacity. We're trying to ramp this thing very quickly."

And on the CPO laser opportunity, which he described as sole-sourced at that moment:

> "We are seeing early shipments. So at least as far as we know, we're sole sourced."

Guidance for the September 2025 quarter called for $510 to $540 million — a midpoint implying 58 percent year-over-year growth. The company delivered $533.8 million, with the non-GAAP operating margin at 18.7 percent. By the December 2025 quarter, revenue reached $665.5 million — another record — with the non-GAAP gross margin at 42.5 percent and operating margin at 25.2 percent. Hurlston described the OCS backlog as having crossed $400 million, with EML capacity fully booked under long-term agreements through 2027.

On the 1.6-terabit per second transition, he was notably bullish compared to the more cautious framing of prior quarters:

> "It's 1.6T is definitely stronger than we felt, you know, than we felt ninety days ago. So 1.6T is definitely accelerating."

The S&P 500 inclusion, effective 23 March 2026, arrived shortly after.

## $808 million and the NVIDIA imprimatur

On 2 March 2026, NVIDIA announced a $2 billion strategic investment in Lumentum alongside a multibillion-dollar purchase commitment, designating the company as a standard supplier for the Rubin architecture platform. Jensen Huang called it a partnership to advance "the world's most sophisticated silicon photonics to build the next generation of gigawatt-scale AI factories." Hurlston's statement characterised it as a multiyear accord reflecting "our shared commitment to advancing the optics technologies that will power the next generation of AI infrastructure." The $2.02 billion cash arrived on the balance sheet in time to be reflected in the March 2026 quarter results, bringing total cash and short-term investments to $3.17 billion.

The March 2026 quarter — Hurlston's fourth full earnings cycle — produced $808.4 million in revenue, a 90 percent year-over-year advance that shattered every internal record. The non-GAAP gross margin expanded a further 540 basis points sequentially to 47.9 percent. Components revenue, which incorporated the EML and laser chip businesses, grew 77 percent year-over-year to $533 million, driven by pump lasers up 80 percent annually and narrow linewidth laser assemblies up more than 120 percent — the ninth consecutive quarter of growth for that product line. Systems revenue, the segment encompassing cloud transceivers and OCS modules, advanced 121 percent year-over-year.

The supply constraint narrative that had threaded through every call since late 2024 had by this point hardened into a structural feature rather than a transitional inconvenience:

> "Supply-demand imbalance appears to have increased to somewhere greater than 30%."

In a television interview the same week, Hurlston compressed the situation to a single sentence: *"We're sold out really until the end of 2027. We see no end in sight."*

Guidance issued for the June 2026 quarter pointed to $960 million to $1.01 billion in revenue at a 35 to 36 percent non-GAAP operating margin — a threshold that, if the midpoint held, would put Lumentum within reach of the $2 billion quarterly revenue trajectory Hurlston had begun publicly invoking. The company that Lowe had carried through the JDSU spin-off, the Oclaro acquisition and the Apple peak had, under its new chief executive's first full fiscal year, more than doubled its quarterly revenue and nearly tripled its operating margin from the trough it recorded twelve months prior.

chapters.title: Hurlston, Wajid Ali CFO, and the Herscher-chaired board
chapters.body:
## A Franchise in Transition

When Lumentum's board announced in February 2025 that Michael Hurlston would become the company's president and chief executive officer, it closed a nine-year era during which Alan Lowe had run the optical-components business — first at JDS Uniphase before the August 2015 spin-off, then through the Oclaro and NeoPhotonics acquisitions, the Apple 3D-sensing surge, and finally the most severe telecom inventory correction in decades. The transition, described in the company's 2025 proxy statement as "the first CEO transition in [Lumentum's] history as a standalone company," was not a crisis succession but a deliberate board pivot toward a leader equipped to exploit the AI and datacenter inflection that the company's technology stack was beginning to capture.

> "We entered the year with clarity, discipline, and a renewed focus on execution. We not only delivered strong results but also positioned Lumentum at the center of one of the most profound technology transformations of our time."

So wrote Hurlston and independent chair Penelope Herscher, jointly, in the October 2025 annual proxy letter to shareholders. That letter also offered a valediction for Lowe: "We would also like to take a moment to thank Alan Lowe for his nearly 10 years at the helm of Lumentum. He spun the Company out of JDS Uniphase and built the foundation that we are now carrying forward."

## Michael Hurlston: Three-Platform Pedigree

Hurlston's biography, as disclosed in the [2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000130817925000615/lite014752-def14a.htm), is more directly relevant to the optical-components industry than the prep-data summary suggests. He holds a B.S. and M.S. in Electrical Engineering plus an M.B.A., all from the University of California, Davis. His career began at Broadcom Limited, where he spent sixteen years (November 2001 to October 2017) in progressively senior roles — rising to senior vice president and general manager of the Mobile Connectivity Products and Wireless Communications and Connectivity division, with an intermediate stretch as executive vice president of sales. That tenure produced deep expertise in high-volume mixed-signal product execution at volume customers, which would later inform his cost-discipline framing at Lumentum.

What the prep data underweights is the intervening chapter. Between Broadcom and Synaptics, Hurlston served as chief executive officer of **Finisar Corporation** from January 2018 to August 2019 — during which he oversaw the company's negotiated sale to II-VI Incorporated (now Coherent). Finisar was at the time one of the world's largest manufacturers of optical communications components and modules, a direct antecedent to the market Lumentum occupies. Hurlston therefore arrived at Lumentum not merely as a semiconductor and IoT executive, but as a CEO who had already navigated the optical-components supply chain, customer base, and competitive dynamics from the inside of a direct peer.

After Finisar, Hurlston led Synaptics Incorporated from August 2019 to February 2025, executing a strategic repositioning away from the PC and mobile touchpad business toward IoT connectivity and edge-AI applications. The Synaptics tenure established his public-company credibility on transformation execution — which was precisely the mandate he carried into Lumentum.

The board conducted "an extensive CEO search process involving the full Board, supported by an executive recruitment team" that evaluated both internal and external candidates, according to the 2025 proxy. Its conclusion was unambiguous: "The Board unanimously determined that Michael Hurlston would be the right CEO at this critical and exciting period for Lumentum," citing "his unique blend of public company leadership experience in the photonics industry as well as in the semiconductor space, and his vision for the future of the global photonics industry and Lumentum's place in it."

Effective February 7, 2025, Hurlston assumed the president and CEO role and was simultaneously appointed to the board of directors, where he holds no committee seat. Alongside Lumentum he sits on the boards of Flex Ltd. (since September 2020) and Astera Labs (since September 2022), providing cross-reference into the EMS and AI connectivity ecosystems that are core to hyperscaler infrastructure.

## The CFO Anchor: Wajid Ali Since February 2019

Wajid Ali joined Lumentum as executive vice president and chief financial officer in February 2019, giving him more than six years of continuity across the NeoPhotonics integration, the telecom downturn, and the AI-inflection revival. His biography, from the [same 2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000130817925000615/lite014752-def14a.htm), traces an earlier Synaptics connection: he was senior vice president and CFO at Synaptics from May 2015 to February 2019 — departing exactly when he joined Lumentum, though Hurlston would not arrive at Synaptics until August of that year. Before Synaptics, Ali was vice president and controller at Teledyne Technologies, and before Teledyne served as CFO of DALSA Corp. (a semiconductor company acquired by Teledyne in 2011). He also held senior finance roles at Advanced Micro Devices and ATI Technologies. He holds BA and MA degrees in Economics from York University, an MBA from the Schulich School of Business at York, and CPA, CMA designations from the Chartered Professional Accountants of Ontario. Since May 2024 he has served as a board director of TTM Technologies, the printed circuit board manufacturer.

Ali's institutional continuity has been the financial-architecture bridge through every phase of Lumentum's recent history. The 2025 proxy's compensation tables show his base salary at $556,000 for FY2025, consistent with the prior year, reflecting a stable-compensation posture at the CFO level through the CEO transition. On May 5, 2026, Ali signed the Q3 FY26 earnings 8-K as chief financial officer, attesting to his uninterrupted stewardship of the finance function across the leadership handoff.

## The Operating Architecture

The executive layer beneath Hurlston and Ali has been reorganised materially relative to the pre-transition structure. The current [leadership roster as disclosed on lumentum.com](https://www.lumentum.com/en/about-us/company/leadership) lists thirteen executives, including a newly created Chief Transformation Officer (Michael Brooker) and Chief Strategy Officer/Chief Marketing Officer (Rafik Ward), reflecting Hurlston's emphasis on operational rigour and go-to-market sharpening.

The most strategically significant operating appointment is **Wupen Yuen**, who carries the title President, Global Business Units. Yuen's biography, per the 2025 proxy, is rooted in NeoPhotonics, where he served as chief product officer (2018–2022) and senior vice president and general manager (2014–2018) before Lumentum's August 2022 acquisition brought him into the company. Prior to NeoPhotonics he was CTO of Bandwidth9, a tunable laser startup. He holds a PhD and master's degree in Electrical Engineering from Stanford and a bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from National Taiwan University. His elevation to a "President" designation signals the breadth of his portfolio responsibility as Lumentum scales its 800G transceiver and emerging 1.6T transceiver product lines — the latter targeted for a Q4 FY2026 production ramp with integrated internal CW lasers, per Q3 FY26 earnings materials.

Vincent Retort, EVP for Modules R&D and New Product Design and Development, is a Lumentum founding-era executive who has held operating, R&D, and business-unit leadership roles continuously since the 2015 JDSU spin. His institutional knowledge of the indium phosphide manufacturing process, 3D sensing, and coherent transmission product lines provides engineering continuity under the new CEO.

## Penelope Herscher: The Decade-Long Chair

Penelope A. Herscher has chaired the Lumentum board since its formation as a public company in August 2015, making her tenure coincident with the company's entire independent existence. Her biography in the 2025 proxy describes "more than 15 years of experience as a high-tech CEO in Silicon Valley and more than 15 years of experience serving on public company boards." She was president and CEO of FirstRain, an enterprise software company, from 2004 to 2015; CEO of Simplex Solutions from 1996 to 2002, taking it public in 2001 and overseeing its sale to Cadence Design Systems in 2002; and held executive roles at Cadence (executive vice president and CMO, 2002–2003) and Synopsys before that. She holds a BA Hons and MA in Mathematics from Cambridge University. As of the 2025 proxy she also chairs the board of Penguin Solutions and sits on the board of Forvia SE.

The board's own governance disclosure in the 2025 proxy articulates her role: Herscher "assists in developing the agenda for the board meetings, is the primary liaison between the board of directors and management, chairs meetings of the board of directors and executive sessions and assists with stockholder communications as requested." During the CEO search and transition, her combination of EDA/SaaS operating experience and decade of optical-components-industry governance depth made her the natural fulcrum for a process that required industry credibility, board-process authority, and external-candidate evaluation discipline simultaneously.

## The Board: Composition and Strategic Logic

| Director | Primary Occupation | Director Since | Key Committee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Penelope A. Herscher | Advisor/Former CEO (FirstRain, Simplex) | Aug 2015 | Governance (Chair) |
| Brian J. Lillie | Former President, Private Cloud, Rackspace Technology | Aug 2015 | Compensation |
| Ian S. Small | CEO, Blues Inc. | Dec 2018 | Compensation (Chair) |
| Julia S. Johnson | Former SVP/GM, Zebra Technologies | Nov 2017 | Audit; Governance |
| Isaac H. Harris | Founder/CEO, DATKI Partners | Jun 2021 | Compensation |
| Pamela F. Fletcher | CEO, Sion Power Corporation | Feb 2023 | Audit; Governance |
| Paul R. Lundstrom | CFO, Copeland LP | Dec 2024 | Audit (Chair) |
| Michael E. Hurlston | President & CEO, Lumentum | Feb 2025 | None (executive) |

*Source: [Lumentum 2025 DEF 14A](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000130817925000615/lite014752-def14a.htm), filed October 7, 2025*

The board was refreshed materially over the 2024–2025 period. Janet S. Wong did not stand for re-election at the November 2024 annual meeting; Harold L. Covert served through FY2025 on the Audit Committee but did not stand for re-election at the November 2025 meeting. Paul Lundstrom, the active CFO of Copeland LP who previously served as CFO of Flex Ltd. from 2020 to 2024, joined in December 2024 to chair the Audit Committee — bringing current large-cap financial-controller discipline at precisely the moment the company's revenue and cash-generation profile were scaling toward a more complex capital-structure environment. (In March 2026 Lumentum raised approximately $2 billion through a Series A Convertible Preferred Stock issuance, lifting total cash to $3.2 billion at the end of Q3 FY26.)

Ian Small's presence traces to the Oclaro acquisition: he had been an Oclaro director from September 2017 until December 2018, when Lumentum closed the $1.8 billion purchase, giving him a perspective on the combined entity's technology base from the acquired side. He chairs the Compensation Committee, which managed the financial architecture of the CEO transition — including Lowe's transition agreement providing for board service through June 30, 2025 and part-time advisory service through December 15, 2025.
