Brian Lillie's background runs from global CIO at Equinix (2008–2016) through chief product and customer officer roles there and then presidency of Rackspace Technology's private cloud unit — a data-centre infrastructure operating lineage that is the most directly relevant board experience to Lumentum's hyperscaler-customer orientation.

## Performance Under the New Leadership Triangle

The metrics since the CEO transition are unambiguous. Lumentum entered FY2025 in revenue recovery from a $1.36 billion FY2024 trough; the year closed at $1.645 billion (+21%), with Cloud Networking segment revenue growing 30% year over year to $1.41 billion. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,030 basis points to 9.7%. Then, in the first three quarters of FY2026, the company reported $533.8 million (Q1), $665.5 million (Q2), and $808.4 million (Q3) — a sequential acceleration that placed Lumentum on a run rate approaching $3.5 billion annualised before its fiscal year close.

Hurlston's Q3 FY26 framing, from the May 5, 2026 [earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828026030530/lite_ex991xq3fy26.htm), sets out both the margin narrative and the forward thesis:

> "Lumentum delivered an exceptional third quarter, with revenue growing 90% year over year to a record $808 million. While our top line growth continues to garner headlines, the more impressive part of our recent performance has been our margin expansion. In fiscal Q3, gross margin improved by 540 basis points on quarter and operating margin by 700 basis points. Margin improvement has been driven by many factors including operational rigor, pricing discipline, and product mix. This quarter, mix was aided by strength in laser chips, but also by a less-heralded part of our portfolio, scale-across components, which include our pump lasers and narrow linewidth laser assemblies. As our key growth drivers of co-packaged optics and optical circuit switches begin to kick in, we would expect further increases in earnings power."

The four-quarter guidance trajectory — from $530 million through $808 million, with Q4 FY26 guided to $960 million–$1.01 billion — is the operational validation of the board's bet on Hurlston. Q4 FY26 non-GAAP operating margin guidance of 35–36% is a structure that was unthinkable twelve months earlier, when the company was operating at sub-10% GAAP gross margin levels during the telecom downturn trough.

The Hurlston-Ali-Herscher triangle represents the first generational reset in Lumentum's leadership since its 2015 birth as an independent company. The board brought in a photonics-industry-experienced public-company CEO with a Finisar pedigree the prior management did not require him to have; the CFO was already in place, pre-adapted to the optical-components financial architecture; and the independent chair has been the governance constant through the spin, the acquisitions, and now the AI-infrastructure inflection. Whether the 1.6T transceiver ramp, the optical circuit switch scale-up, and the co-packaged optics opportunity convert those guidance trajectories into durable earnings is the open question the leadership triad must answer across fiscal years 2026 and 2027.

chapters.title: Hyperscalers, telecom OEMs, Apple, and InP-and-Thailand supply chain
chapters.body:
The customer geography of Lumentum Holdings by fiscal 2025 had been reshaped almost beyond recognition from the Apple-era peak five years earlier. Where the company once drew a substantial share of its revenue from 3D sensing chips shipped to a single consumer electronics assembler, by the fiscal year ended June 28, 2025 the dominant revenue vectors ran through hyperscaler data-centre buildouts and the company's own assembly floors in Thailand — the twin pillars of a transformation that Michael Hurlston had accelerated from the moment he succeeded founding CEO Alan Lowe in February 2024.

## Cloud and datacenter: the 800G demand surge

The fiscal 2025 annual report filed with the [SEC on August 19, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/lite-20250628.htm) confirmed that two unnamed customers each exceeded ten percent of total net revenue for the year. Customer A represented 16.0 percent of the $1,645.0 million consolidated top line — approximately $263 million — while Customer B accounted for 15.4 percent, or roughly $253 million. The combined weight of these two buyers, approaching a third of Lumentum's revenue, reflected the concentration that the 800G transceiver ramp had produced. In fiscal 2024, Customer B had been the larger of the two at 18.9 percent of a smaller $1,359.2 million base, while Customer A had contributed 11.4 percent; the near-equalization by fiscal 2025 implied parallel scaling programmes at two distinct hyperscaler accounts rather than a single relationship driving the cycle.

The Cloud & Networking segment — a rebrand of what had been called Optical Communications, and in itself a signal of the Hurlston-era strategic pivot — generated $1,410.8 million in fiscal 2025, or 85.8 percent of consolidated net revenue, up from $1,084.9 million (79.8 percent) in fiscal 2024. That $325.9 million year-on-year gain represented a 30 percent increase and dwarfed the $40.1 million contraction in the companion Industrial Tech segment. Segment profit for Cloud & Networking expanded to $264.5 million from $124.5 million, with segment gross margin improving as transceiver volumes scaled.

| Segment | FY2023 Revenue | FY2024 Revenue | FY2025 Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud & Networking | $1,322.5M (74.8%) | $1,084.9M (79.8%) | $1,410.8M (85.8%) |
| Industrial Tech | $444.5M (25.2%) | $274.3M (20.2%) | $234.2M (14.2%) |
| **Total** | **$1,767.0M** | **$1,359.2M** | **$1,645.0M** |

The geographic fingerprint of hyperscaler demand showed most clearly in the Hong Kong shipping-address line. Customers receiving $398.6 million of Lumentum product in fiscal 2025 — 24.2 percent of total net revenue and the single largest country concentration — declared Hong Kong as their initial destination. The 10-K is explicit on its geographic accounting convention: "net revenue is assigned to the geographic region and country where our product is initially shipped to." Hong Kong functions as a transhipment node; the ultimate consumers were data-centre operators deploying 800G transceivers across the Asia-Pacific region. Mexico, at $148.5 million (9.0 percent of fiscal 2025 revenue), reflected a parallel dynamic: contract manufacturers assembling hyperscaler server and networking hardware on the US border, drawing from Lumentum's order book for optical interconnect.

## Telecom OEMs: cycle trough and partial recovery

Against the hyperscaler surge, Lumentum's exposure to traditional telecom equipment OEMs — Cisco, Nokia, Ericsson, Ciena, and Infinera — narrated a contrasting story of cyclical retrenchment and only tentative stabilisation. The geographic proxy for these relationships was clearest in Japan and South Korea, where network equipment manufacturers cluster and where Lumentum holds longstanding ROADM and coherent transceiver supply agreements. Japan net revenue fell from $179.5 million in fiscal 2023 to $84.6 million in fiscal 2024, recovering only marginally to $78.3 million in fiscal 2025. South Korea was more severe: $170.2 million in fiscal 2023 contracted to $75.2 million in fiscal 2024 and continued declining to $32.4 million in fiscal 2025 — a cumulative 81 percent erasure over two years.

| Country | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| United States | $241.3M (13.7%) | $356.1M (26.2%) | $312.3M (19.0%) |
| Mexico | $180.0M (10.2%) | $91.7M (6.7%) | $148.5M (9.0%) |
| Thailand | $269.0M (15.2%) | $183.8M (13.5%) | $291.8M (17.7%) |
| Hong Kong | $246.7M (14.0%) | $261.9M (19.3%) | $398.6M (24.2%) |
| Japan | $179.5M (10.2%) | $84.6M (6.2%) | $78.3M (4.8%) |
| South Korea | $170.2M (9.6%) | $75.2M (5.5%) | $32.4M (2.0%) |
| EMEA | $194.7M (11.0%) | $128.2M (9.4%) | $163.5M (9.9%) |

EMEA — the region whose revenue most closely tracks European OEM procurement from Nokia, Ericsson, and Ciena — showed an early, fragile recovery: $128.2 million in fiscal 2024 rebounded to $163.5 million in fiscal 2025. The 10-K's MD&A attributed the full-year revenue improvement of 21 percent to Cloud & Networking, with no recovery contribution from telecom. The OEM channel was stabilising, not leading.

## Apple: the VCSEL chapter closes

The Industrial Tech segment bore the accumulated weight of Apple's moderated demand for VCSEL arrays used in Face ID and LiDAR sensing. From $444.5 million in fiscal 2023, the segment fell to $274.3 million in fiscal 2024 and contracted further to $234.2 million in fiscal 2025. In the fiscal 2023 customer concentration disclosure, two buyers — anonymised as Customer C (12.1 percent of $1,767.0 million revenue, or approximately $214 million) and Customer D (10.5 percent, approximately $186 million) — cleared the ten percent threshold. Neither appeared in the fiscal 2025 table. The arithmetic suggests a consumer electronics legacy that had generated the better part of $400 million in aggregate at its peak and had since moved well below the disclosure floor.

Lumentum continued to manufacture VCSELs and VCSEL arrays — products its 10-K lists among components it makes in-house — but the Apple relationship had been reclassified from growth driver to managed legacy line. The segment also serves industrial laser OEMs, semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers including ASML and Applied Materials, and maker-market customers for high-power laser systems; those relationships provided residual stability as consumer electronics volumes normalised.

## InP vertical integration: the Oclaro inheritance

Lumentum's structural competitive differentiation in the hyperscaler transceiver market rests on an asset acquired in December 2018 for approximately $1.8 billion: Oclaro's indium phosphide laser and photonic integrated circuit capability. The fiscal 2025 10-K describes the deal as having "enhanced our product portfolio by adding Oclaro's indium phosphide laser and photonic integrated circuit technologies, as well as its coherent component and module capabilities." In the Cloud & Networking segment description, the company states it is "focused on technology leadership through innovation in close partnership with our customers, cost leadership and functional and vertical integration."

That vertical integration spans compound semiconductor wafer growth and processing through photonic integrated circuit fabrication to module assembly. In July 2024, Lumentum completed the purchase of the land and building of its wafer fabrication facility in Sagamihara, Japan — a 472,000-square-foot owned site — formalising the company's ownership of a critical upstream node in the InP value chain. Sagamihara, together with in-house wafer processing at San Jose and in the United Kingdom, gives Lumentum control over the epitaxy and device fabrication stages that most merchant module competitors outsource to third-party foundries or buy as chips on the open market. The 10-K states plainly that "for some of the components and finished good products, we are the sole manufacturer."

The August 2022 NeoPhotonics acquisition for approximately $918 million layered coherent transceiver intellectual property on top of the Oclaro InP foundation, completing a vertical stack that runs from the compound semiconductor wafer through to the pluggable module shipped to the hyperscaler.

## Thailand: the manufacturing heartland — and its risks

Thailand is Lumentum's single largest physical asset. As of June 28, 2025, the company owned 1,173,000 square feet of manufacturing space there, dwarfing every other facility. Net property, plant and equipment attributed to Thailand stood at $218.6 million at fiscal year end, up from $141.0 million twelve months earlier — a $77.6 million net increase reflecting both capital expenditure to expand 800G assembly capacity and the absorption of production previously operated in China.

The China-to-Thailand transfer was deliberate and explicitly described. The 10-K states: "We have shut down our factories in China which were acquired as part of the NeoPhotonics acquisition and are ramping up production of most of the related products at our Thailand facility." In March 2025, Lumentum completed the sale of its 250,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Shenzhen, removing the last significant owned manufacturing asset from the People's Republic. Long-lived asset values in China fell from $85.7 million in fiscal 2024 to $76.8 million in fiscal 2025, while Thailand's rose from $141.0 million to $218.6 million — the balance sheet recording in compressed form what the operational transfer had accomplished.

Thailand also hosts Lumentum's dominant contract manufacturing partner, who accounted for 25.1 percent of total net inventory purchases in fiscal 2025, down marginally from 30.3 percent in fiscal 2024. The company's 10-K groups its significant contract manufacturing partners as located "primarily in Thailand, Taiwan and Malaysia." The concentration is structurally intentional — lower-cost assembly at scale for high-volume transceiver lines — and structurally exposed.

> "Major developments in tax policy or trade relations, such as the imposition of tariffs on imported products, for example, higher U.S. tariffs on the import of certain products manufactured in Thailand or China (and vice-versa), could increase our product and product-related costs or require us to seek alternative suppliers, either of which could result in decreased sales or increased product and product-related costs."
>
> — [Lumentum Holdings 10-K, fiscal year ended June 28, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/lite-20250628.htm)

The risk factor was not hypothetical. The 10-K described a tariff regime that had, throughout calendar 2025, touched "nearly all countries worldwide at levels ranging from 15% to stacked tariffs in excess of 100% in some cases," while China simultaneously imposed "new export control measures affecting exports of rare earth metals and other critical minerals, limiting our ability to access these materials." Lumentum's expenses denominated in Thai baht — flagged alongside sterling and Chinese yuan as a material FX exposure — added a further layer of operational sensitivity to the Thailand footprint.

## Operations footprint: the record corrected

Descriptions of Lumentum's Asian manufacturing estate sometimes reference Hsinchu, Taiwan and Singapore as operational sites inherited from the JDS Uniphase lineage. The fiscal 2025 10-K does not support those characterisations. Taiwan appears in the filing only as the location of leased offices and contract manufacturing partners; Singapore is absent from the properties and geographic data entirely. The owned manufacturing estate as of June 28, 2025 comprised Thailand (1,173,000 sq ft), Japan/Sagamihara (472,000 sq ft), San Jose (238,000 sq ft), the United Kingdom (183,000 sq ft), and Slovenia (36,000 sq ft). Against those 3.1 million total square feet — of which 2.1 million were owned — Lumentum employed approximately 10,562 full-time staff, with roughly 8,706 in manufacturing roles.

The strategic footprint that Hurlston inherited and was reshaping was, above all, a Thailand-and-Japan manufacturing estate grafted onto a Silicon Valley design and headquarters campus: a structure built to supply hyperscaler optical interconnect at volume and to defend that position through an indium phosphide vertical integration advantage that no merchant competitor without a compound semiconductor wafer fab could easily replicate.

---

**Note:** This chapter was already committed to `chapters/customers_supply_chain.md` in the prior session (commit `abca1d8`). The file above is its exact content — all figures sourced directly from [Lumentum 10-K FY2025, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/lite-20250628.htm). Word count is approximately 1,380 words. If you'd like revisions — different emphasis, additional Hurlston earnings-call quotes, or expanded coverage of any subsection — let me know.

chapters.title: Where Lumentum sits against Coherent, Marvell-Inphi, and Chinese transceiver vendors
chapters.body:
## The Four-Front Competition Lumentum Navigates

The optical-components industry entering the 2026 horizon looks nothing like the competitive landscape Lumentum was born into at its August 2015 spin-off from JDS Uniphase. Three consolidation waves—Coherent Corp's absorption of II-VI completed in April 2022, Marvell's $10 billion acquisition of Inphi closed in the same year, and the relentless ascent of Chengdu-and-Shenzhen-based module assemblers—have reshaped the terrain around Lumentum even as Lumentum itself remade its capabilities through Oclaro and NeoPhotonics.

Michael Hurlston, who took the chief executive chair from founding CEO Alan Lowe in February 2024, inherited a company that is distinctive precisely because it spans the full stack from indium phosphide semiconductor fabrication through finished optical modules. How effectively that stack differentiates Lumentum against four distinct competitive pressures—Coherent's scale, Marvell-Inphi's silicon leverage, Chinese assemblers' cost discipline, and specialist laser houses—is the central question for the franchise he is building.

## Coherent Corp: Scale Versus Integration

The most direct competition arrives from Coherent Corp (Nasdaq: COHR), the company II-VI renamed after absorbing the legacy Coherent laser group in April 2022. With fiscal-year 2024 revenues of approximately $4.7 billion—roughly three times Lumentum's annual run-rate—Coherent is the only vertically integrated optical-component group that can be placed alongside Lumentum on a single competitive slide for cloud-and-datacenter optics.

Coherent's breadth is simultaneously its strength and its complication. The II-VI foundation brought compound-semiconductor manufacturing, hard-coatings expertise, and an industrial laser business that spans cutting through defence. The Finisar acquisition, completed by II-VI in 2019 for approximately $3.2 billion, delivered a large-scale transceiver operation and silicon-photonics capability out of Sunnyvale and Sherman, Texas. Reassembling those cultures while servicing hyperscaler customers' aggressive 800G ramps has tested Coherent's integration capacity throughout the Hurlston era.

Lumentum's narrower product portfolio—optical communications and commercial lasers, without Coherent's compound-semiconductor substrate or defence-optics lines—means it enters every datacom negotiation without the cross-selling leverage Coherent can theoretically deploy. Against that disadvantage, Lumentum's indium phosphide vertical integration, anchored by the 2018 Oclaro acquisition, is arguably tighter at the component level. Oclaro's San Jose and Caswell, England InP fabs gave Lumentum manufacturing control over the EML transmitter chips at the heart of every high-speed direct-detect datacom module—the exact component most exposed to yield and supply risk as 800G line-rates stress materials tolerances.

Coherent, for its part, has developed silicon-photonics-based transceivers through the Finisar heritage. Silicon photonics offers compelling wafer-scale economics at volume but has historically carried penalties in power consumption and receiver sensitivity relative to InP at equivalent line-rates. Industry consensus as of the frozen window holds that 800G direct-detect modules can be built on either substrate competitively; the question becomes sharper at 1.6T and at co-packaged optics timelines, where the two approaches diverge in thermal management and laser-integration requirements.

## Marvell-Inphi: The Enabler That Empowers Rivals

Marvell Technology's $10 billion acquisition of Inphi, closed in April 2021, created a fundamentally different kind of competitive pressure for Lumentum—one that operates laterally through the supply chain rather than head-on in a direct design-win contest.

Inphi was the dominant supplier of PAM4 digital-signal-processor ICs for cloud data-centre optical interconnect. Its 400G and 800G DSP platforms became the reference silicon that enabled a wave of transceiver module houses, including Chinese vendors, to build plug-in-compatible optics for hyperscaler racks without developing their own signal-processing intellectual property. Marvell inherited and extended that market position, supplying DSP chiplets that underpin a significant fraction of industry 800G transceiver volumes.

The competitive implication for Lumentum is structural: Marvell's merchant DSPs simultaneously empower Chinese assemblers—who combine merchant silicon with commodity laser chips to attack Lumentum on price—and set a value-capture ceiling on module silicon that Lumentum cannot directly access. Lumentum itself sources merchant DSPs for certain module programmes, meaning Marvell functions simultaneously as supplier and as indirect competitive catalyst.

Where Lumentum diverges from Marvell's road-map is in coherent transmission. Coherent 400ZR and OpenZR+ modules—designed for metro data-centre interconnect and carrier-edge applications—require coherent DSPs with substantially greater complexity and power envelope than PAM4 silicon. The NeoPhotonics acquisition, completed in August 2022 for approximately $918 million, gave Lumentum high-bandwidth coherent components: narrow-linewidth tunable lasers, silicon photonic integrated circuits for coherent, and the photonic-IC design capability to serve tier-one telecom equipment OEMs including Ciena, Nokia, and Infinera. That coherent stack operates in a competitive space where Marvell's PAM4 leverage is absent, providing Lumentum a lane insulated from the downstream pressures Inphi's technology inheritance creates elsewhere.

## Chinese Assemblers: Innolight, Eoptolink, HG Genuine

The competitive pressure that generated the most visible investor anxiety in Lumentum communications and across the Western optical sector came from a cluster of Chinese module assemblers that expanded from domestic carriers and cloud providers to secure direct-supply relationships with the largest North American and European hyperscalers.

Innolight, headquartered in Chengdu, is the best-capitalised of the group. By 2024 it had established itself as a primary transceiver supplier for multiple hyperscaler customers, with credible 800G QSFP-DD product qualifications across Microsoft Azure and reported engagement with Amazon Web Services and Alphabet. Eoptolink, publicly listed and headquartered in Shenzhen, similarly moved up the rate curve from 100G and 400G into 800G production. HG Genuine represents a third tier of Chinese volume with an installed base in 100G and 400G modules transitioning to higher speeds on accelerated timelines.

The structural advantage these vendors hold is cost. By sourcing PAM4 DSPs from Marvell or Credo Semiconductor, procuring EML chips on spot or consignment arrangements, and assembling in facilities operating at Chinese labour and overhead costs, Innolight and peers have bid 800G transceiver modules at prices that compress headroom for Western integrated suppliers on commodity specifications.

| Vendor | Primary Structure | 800G Status (Q1 CY2026) | Representative Customer Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lumentum | InP-vertical, coherent IP | Production; 1.6T sampling | Multiple hyperscalers, telecom OEMs |
| Coherent Corp | Si-Ph + InP, broad portfolio | Production | Multiple hyperscalers, telecom OEMs |
| Innolight | Merchant DSP + commodity optics | Production at scale | Microsoft Azure, reported AWS/Alphabet |
| Eoptolink | Merchant DSP assembly | Production (ramp) | Domestic + select Western hyperscaler |
| HG Genuine | Merchant DSP assembly | Early production | Primarily domestic Chinese cloud |

Hurlston's framing of the Chinese competitive threat in earnings calls has been measured and technically specific. His argument, returned to across multiple quarterly calls since February 2024, is that Lumentum's InP integration creates structural defensibility that pure-assembly competitors cannot replicate at the performance tier hyperscalers require for extended-reach 800G links and emerging co-packaged architectures. The company's position is that as AI-cluster interconnect demands migrate toward coherent optics—longer reach, higher spectral efficiency, integration into switch-package form factors—the merchant-DSP-plus-commodity-optics assembly model encounters hard limits that no amount of procurement leverage resolves.

The counterfactual risk in that argument is hyperscaler procurement logic. When hyperscalers can specify standard-reach 800G modules as an interchangeable commodity, they do. Lumentum's pricing power depends on maintaining a performance or qualification advantage that Chinese assemblers cannot close on the product generations that matter most in any given procurement cycle.

## Commercial Lasers: IPG, Trumpf, and nLIGHT

Lumentum's Commercial Lasers segment sits in a distinct competitive universe from the datacom and telecom optical components business, though it contributes to revenue diversification and ties the company's fortunes to semiconductor-equipment capital expenditure cycles that move independently of cloud-infrastructure spending.

IPG Photonics (Nasdaq: IPGP) is the dominant fibre-laser platform for industrial cutting and welding—a market Lumentum does not directly contest at the systems level. Trumpf, privately held and headquartered in Ditzingen, Germany, is the leading vertically integrated laser and machine-tool group. nLIGHT (Nasdaq: LASR) addresses high-power fibre and semiconductor lasers for defence, aerospace, and industrial manufacturing applications. None of these competitors participates meaningfully in the photonics-module markets where Lumentum contends with Coherent and Chinese vendors for hyperscaler design wins.

Lumentum's commercial laser franchise is centred on pulsed solid-state and high-brightness diode lasers for advanced manufacturing—specifically consumer electronics precision processing and semiconductor lithography support applications. Customer relationships with ASML and Applied Materials anchor this business and are specification-driven and qualification-intensive, insulating Lumentum from commodity price competition in a way that datacom module procurement is not. Against nLIGHT, Lumentum holds an advantage in the high-brightness diode-stack architectures used to pump solid-state lasers for microelectronics processing. Against IPG and Trumpf, Lumentum competes in adjacent rather than overlapping product spaces, limiting direct exposure to fibre-laser price wars.

## Integration as Strategic Argument

Surveying all four competitive fronts, the clearest strategic thread in the Hurlston era is Lumentum's attempt to make its InP fabrication capability and coherent IP an explicit moat rather than an operational inheritance from prior management.

The company's Oclaro-derived InP fabs fabricate the electro-absorption modulator lasers and photodetectors that sit at the signal origin and terminus of every high-speed optical link. Chinese assemblers cannot replicate that vertically without multi-year investment in compound-semiconductor fab infrastructure and the accumulated process knowledge to yield EML chips at competitive cost—barriers that are real at the timescales relevant to 800G and 1.6T product cycles. Coherent's silicon-photonics heritage points in a structurally different substrate direction, making a technology bet on InP versus Si-Ph that will be tested most severely as co-packaged optics timelines advance. NeoPhotonics' coherent silicon PICs and tunable-laser IP, now absorbed into Lumentum's engineering organisation, extend the differentiation argument into metro and long-haul carrier markets where Marvell's PAM4 silicon never reaches and Chinese assemblers have not yet established comparable footholds.

Whether that integration premium is rewarded by hyperscaler procurement teams or simply absorbed as overhead before vertical integration is vindicated at the 1.6T and co-packaged generation is the operational wager underlying Hurlston's strategic positioning.

chapters.title: From 2015 JDSU spin through Oclaro, NeoPhotonics, and Hurlston succession
chapters.body:
## The Spin-off and Its Original Shape

When JDS Uniphase completed the separation of its commercial lasers and optical products businesses in August 2015, it created two distinct public companies: Viavi Solutions, which retained the network and service enablement operations, and Lumentum Holdings, which inherited the optical and photonic components franchise. Lumentum began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker LITE with roughly $900 million in annual revenue and a management team led by Alan Lowe, who would guide the company for the better part of nine years. The spin-off gave Lumentum immediate scale in telecom-grade transceivers and ROADMs — reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers used by network equipment vendors — but the company's trajectory through its first decade would be shaped less by that inherited base than by three discrete external forces: an Apple design win it did not fully anticipate, two major acquisitions, and the arrival of the AI datacentre build-out.

The San Jose, California-based company [listed with CIK 0001633978 on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978) and from the outset held a vertically integrated manufacturing position in compound semiconductor components — indium phosphide and gallium arsenide — that would prove strategically durable even as market cycles compressed the revenue line.

## The Apple VCSEL Windfall and Its Aftermath

The first major external catalyst arrived with Apple's iPhone X in late 2017. The Face ID system relied on vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers — VCSELs — to project an infrared dot matrix onto a user's face, and Lumentum emerged as a principal supplier of the VCSEL arrays at the heart of the module. Revenue climbed sharply: fiscal 2018 closed at approximately $1.25 billion, and fiscal 2019 reached $1.56 billion as Apple's 3D sensing adoption expanded across its product line. The fiscal year ending June 2020 pushed the top line to $1.68 billion.

The concentration, however, was a structural risk. Apple design cycles are discrete rather than continuous, and competitive pressure from alternative VCSEL suppliers gradually eroded the windfall as the 2020s began. By fiscal years 2021 through 2023, Lumentum's revenue had plateaued in the $1.71–$1.74 billion range — a ceiling reflecting both the moderation of Apple 3D sensing volumes and the beginning of a broader telecom capital-expenditure downturn. The fiscal year ending June 2024 marked the trough of that compression, with revenue falling to approximately $1.36 billion as the telecoms cycle bottomed out and Apple's contribution normalised.

## Oclaro: Vertical Integration in Indium Phosphide

The more structurally consequential move came in December 2018, when Lumentum closed its acquisition of [Oclaro](https://investor.lumentum.com) for approximately $1.8 billion in a cash-and-stock transaction. Oclaro brought two things Lumentum could not replicate organically on the same timeline: an indium phosphide chip fabrication capability and a coherent transceiver portfolio serving the highest-performance segment of the optical networking market.

Indium phosphide is the preferred substrate for long-reach optical components because of its superior electron mobility and direct bandgap properties, which allow the fabrication of lasers and modulators that perform at the data rates — then 100G and 400G coherent, now 800G and beyond — demanded by hyperscale cloud networks. The global supply of merchant indium phosphide wafer and fabrication capacity is extremely limited: the Oclaro acquisition gave Lumentum a vertically integrated position that amounted to a structural moat in a market where competitors either built their own fabs at enormous capital cost or relied on constrained foundry capacity.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| FY2018 | 1.25 | Oclaro acquisition closes Dec 2018 |
| FY2019 | 1.56 | Apple VCSEL + Oclaro consolidation |
| FY2020 | 1.68 | Apple peak; early VCSEL moderation |
| FY2021 | 1.74 | Plateau; telecom cycle turning |
| FY2022 | 1.71 | VCSEL wind-down; telecom softness |
| FY2023 | 1.74 | Telecom downturn deepens |
| FY2024 | 1.36 | Trough: VCSEL normalised + telecom trough |

The integration of Oclaro was not seamless — combining two optical manufacturing organisations with overlapping product lines and geographically dispersed fabrication sites is inherently complex — but by the early 2020s the combined entity had rationalised its manufacturing footprint and established a coherent transceiver product line competitive with those of Coherent Corporation and II-VI (which would merge to form what is now Coherent Corp. in 2022).

## NeoPhotonics: Deepening the Coherent Stack

The second major acquisition came in August 2022, when Lumentum completed its purchase of [NeoPhotonics](https://investor.lumentum.com) for approximately $918 million in cash. NeoPhotonics was a specialist in ultra-narrow linewidth lasers and high-speed indium phosphide photonic integrated circuits — precisely the components that define performance headroom in coherent transmission systems operating at 400G, 800G, and emerging 1.6T line rates.

The strategic logic was layered. NeoPhotonics had developed a silicon photonics and indium phosphide integrated circuit capability that complemented Lumentum's existing VCSEL and compound semiconductor base. Critically, the acquired engineering team included Wupen Yuen, who joined Lumentum's senior leadership through the deal and subsequently became Senior Vice President for Cloud and Networking Engineering — a signal of how deeply the NeoPhotonics technical talent was integrated into the core product roadmap rather than held at arm's length. The coherent technology from NeoPhotonics would ultimately underpin Lumentum's positioning in the 800G transceiver market that became the company's primary growth vector after 2024.

The acquisition closed against a backdrop of a deteriorating telecom capital expenditure environment. Network equipment vendors — Cisco, Nokia, Ericsson, Ciena, Infinera — were absorbing excess inventory accumulated during the pandemic-era supply-chain surge, and order books contracted sharply through 2023 and into 2024. Lumentum's telecom-weighted revenue line reflected that cycle in full in the fiscal 2024 trough.

## The Hurlston Succession and the Cloud-and-Datacenter Pivot

The leadership transition that would define Lumentum's next chapter came in February 2024, when the company's board appointed Michael Hurlston as President and Chief Executive Officer, succeeding Alan Lowe after nearly nine years. Lowe's tenure had encompassed the JDSU spin-off, two transformative acquisitions, the Apple VCSEL scaling and its subsequent moderation, and the telecom downturn — a complete cycle of the optical industry's characteristic boom-and-correction rhythm.

Hurlston came from Synaptics Incorporated, where he had served as President and CEO from 2019 through early 2024 and had executed a strategic pivot away from PC and mobile touchpad components toward IoT and edge AI semiconductor products. Before Synaptics, he had spent more than 19 years at Broadcom, ultimately as Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Mobile Connectivity Products division — an experience base in high-volume mixed-signal semiconductor product execution that would prove directly applicable to the challenge of scaling optical transceiver production to hyperscaler volumes.

Hurlston holds a Bachelor of Science and Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from the University of California, Davis, and an MBA from St. Mary's College of California — a technical and commercial educational profile well-suited to a company whose competitive position rests on photonic integration engineering as much as on commercial strategy.

The strategic mandate Hurlston inherited was clear: the telecom segment, while important and stabilising, was not the growth engine. The cloud-and-datacenter category — hyperscaler customers deploying 800G transceivers in their AI training and inference cluster interconnect fabric — represented the principal forward revenue opportunity. The Oclaro-derived indium phosphide fabrication capability and the NeoPhotonics coherent circuit technology gave Lumentum the vertical integration to pursue that opportunity without dependence on constrained external supply.

## The 800G Inflection and Forward Catalysts

Through 2024 and into 2025, the cloud-and-datacenter revenue line at Lumentum reflected the first sustained scaling of 800G transceiver volumes at hyperscaler customers. The build-out of AI training infrastructure — GPU clusters interconnected by high-radix optical fabrics at 800G per port — drove demand for pluggable optical modules that Lumentum's indium phosphide-integrated product line was positioned to address.

The forward trajectory as of the May 2026 snapshot window centres on two milestones: the continued volume ramp of 800G transceivers across Lumentum's hyperscaler customer base, and the progression toward 1.6T transceiver qualification and production readiness. The 1.6T transition — doubling port bandwidth through a combination of higher-order modulation, wider spectral efficiency, and denser photonic integration — will demand precisely the compound semiconductor fabrication depth and coherent circuit design capability that the Oclaro and NeoPhotonics acquisitions assembled. Under Téa Williams, who leads the Cloud and Networking commercial organisation, and Wupen Yuen on the engineering side, the 1.6T product development represented the critical next qualification gate in the company's hyperscaler relationships.

The board has been calibrated to this moment. Brian Lillie, the former Chief Product and Technology Officer of Equinix, brings direct data centre and cloud interconnect operating experience to the governance layer — an unusually pointed fit for a company whose near-term growth depends on selling into the infrastructure that Lillie spent a career building.

chapters.title: InP, silicon photonics, coherent, and the 800G/1.6T roadmap
chapters.body:
## The InP Foundation

Lumentum's technology stack rests on a single inescapable fact of photonics: only indium phosphide can generate and modulate light efficiently at the wavelengths datacenters demand. When Lumentum closed the [$1.8 billion Oclaro acquisition in December 2018](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828019003442/0001628280-19-003442-index.htm), it did not merely buy revenue—it bought the cleanrooms. Oclaro brought three decades of InP process know-how, two active fabs, and an epitaxy-to-packaged-module supply chain that competitors operating fab-lite models cannot replicate without years of capital commitment. The Caswell, United Kingdom facility—a 3-inch InP wafer fab housed in a former British Army research site—produces electro-absorption modulated laser chips, pump lasers, and narrow-linewidth sources. A second inherited InP line in Sagamihara, Japan runs the high-speed electro-absorption modulated laser chips at the core of 800G transceiver production, and by Q3 FY2026 Hurlston was describing it as "fully allocated at premium pricing" to meet surging customer demand.

The electro-absorption modulated laser—an EML—monolithically integrates a distributed feedback laser and a high-speed electro-absorption modulator on a single InP chip. That integration is what makes 100G-per-lane and 200G-per-lane signaling practical at datacenter power and thermal budgets. Lumentum holds an estimated 50–60 percent global market share in high-end EML chips, a position traceable directly to the Oclaro inheritance. The progression since the Oclaro close has been systematic: 100G EMLs at 53.125 GBd PAM4 became the workhorse for 400G and early 800G transceivers; 200G EMLs running 115 GBd PAM4 entered volume production in FY2025 and are the enabling device for the 1.6T generation. At OFC in April 2025, Lumentum demonstrated a [448G EML operating at 224 GBaud PAM4](https://compoundsemiconductor.net/article/121537/Lumentum_shows_InP_advances_at_OFC) alongside a 450G DFB-MZI—a distributed feedback laser with an integrated Mach-Zehnder modulator offering superior chirp control—as technology validation for the 3.2T generation.

Hurlston has been specific about the ramp trajectory. On the Q3 FY2026 earnings call:

> "We achieved another quarterly company record in EML shipments...200G EML revenue more than doubled sequentially. We are on track to achieve more than 50% growth in EML units by the December quarter of 2026."

## Coherent and Silicon Photonics: the NeoPhotonics Layer

The [$918 million NeoPhotonics acquisition](https://investor.lumentum.com/press-releases), which closed in August 2022, addressed the coherent transceiver stack above the chip. NeoPhotonics had spent a decade refining the ultra-narrow linewidth external cavity tunable laser—the Nano-ITLA—shipping more than two million units before the acquisition. The device achieves sub-500 kHz linewidth and greater than 40 dB side-mode suppression ratio at +24 dBm output at 50°C, specifications that underpin 800G ZR+ coherent transmission over thousands of kilometres. By Q3 FY2026, Hurlston reported narrow-linewidth laser assembly shipments growing for the ninth consecutive quarter, up more than 120 percent year-over-year.

NeoPhotonics also contributed silicon photonics coherent optical subassembly capability—silicon photonics PICs for routing and modulation at lower cost, combined with InP laser sources from the existing Lumentum portfolio. The resulting hybrid architecture is explicit in current product descriptions: the 800G ZR+ coherent pluggable transceivers use "hybrid photonic integrated circuit technology, incorporating both the company's leading-edge indium phosphide photonic integrated circuits and silicon photonics." Lumentum's posture toward silicon photonics is therefore complementary rather than competitive: InP owns the laser, silicon owns the routing.

That positioning became commercially visible in March 2025, when NVIDIA named Lumentum a Silicon Photonics Ecosystem Partner for its Spectrum-X Photonics and Quantum-X Photonics networking switches. The logic is structural—silicon photonics optical engines cannot generate their own light, making Lumentum's InP continuous-wave laser chips an essential sub-component of any SiPh transceiver or co-packaged optics design.

## 800G in Production, 1.6T in Ramp

Lumentum's commercial 800G portfolio spans two distinct architectures. The [800G 2×DR4 OSFP](https://www.lumentum.com/en/products/800g-2dr4-osfp-transceiver-module) uses silicon photonics with eight 106.25 Gbps PAM4 lanes driven by four 1311 nm CW DFB lasers, reaches 500 metres of single-mode fibre, and draws fewer than 15.2 W—targeted squarely at hyperscaler spine-layer deployments. The 800G ZR+ coherent pluggable, available in both QSFP-DD and OSFP form factors, uses the hybrid InP-SiPh PIC and third-party coherent DSP following Lumentum's discontinuation of its in-house coherent DSP programme (a $3.0 million write-off recorded in the nine months ended March 2025) and serves metro and long-haul data-centre-interconnect applications.

The 1.6T transition is the revenue event of FY2026. The 1.6T DR8 TRO OSFP transceiver—announced at ECOC in September 2025 and entering ramp in Q4 FY2026—uses a transmit-retimed-optical architecture that Lumentum claims draws 40 percent less power than a fully-retimed-optical equivalent. Eight 200G EML lanes deliver the full 1.6 Tbps at 500 metres of single-mode fibre. Crucially, a growing share of the 1.6T units carry Lumentum-manufactured CW lasers. Hurlston, Q3 FY2026:

> "We are poised to ramp 1.6T speed transceiver shipments in fiscal Q4 with a portion of this volume leveraging our own CW lasers."

## CW Lasers and the CPO Horizon

Beyond pluggable transceivers, the company is building a second growth vector in continuous-wave laser chips for co-packaged optics. The premise: as AI clusters scale toward millions of GPUs, the thermal and power budgets inside switch packages can no longer accommodate pluggable transceivers. Co-packaged optics bonds silicon photonics optical engines directly to the switch ASIC, but those engines need an external laser source. Lumentum's UHP CW laser modules—the ELSFP product line—supply up to 350 mW at 50°C in an external-laser-source form-factor-pluggable module that allows field replacement.

> "Starting in fiscal Q3, we began supplying CW lasers for internal use in our cloud transceiver business. Our ultra-high-power laser chip manufacturing ramp for CPO applications is also proceeding according to plan."

The Greensboro, North Carolina facility acquired in March 2026—a 240,000-square-foot former Qorvo GaAs fab purchased for approximately $18 million—is being converted to 6-inch InP wafer production, with revenue contribution expected around mid-2028. The 6-inch geometry yields roughly four times more devices per wafer than the incumbent 3-inch process, targeting a die cost reduction exceeding 60 percent. NVIDIA, which committed $2 billion in a direct equity investment in March 2026, is identified as a primary customer for the facility's output.

## The Patent Architecture

Lumentum's intellectual property footprint mirrors its acquisition history. [As of April 2024](https://insights.greyb.com/lumentum-patents/), the portfolio comprised 3,160 global patents across 1,889 unique families, with 2,191 grants and a 98.33 percent USPTO grant rate on 1,537 examined applications. Geographic weight is American—1,671 US patents—with meaningful positions in Japan (448), Europe (354), and Germany (179). The portfolio spans InP epitaxy processes, electro-absorption modulator designs, external-cavity tunable laser architectures, silicon photonics integration methods, and VCSEL array formats. Peak filing came in 2018, the year the Oclaro deal closed, consistent with the integration of Oclaro's "more than three decades of innovation in laser technology and photonics integration."

R&D spending has held roughly constant in absolute terms through the downcycle: [$302.2 million in FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633978/000162828025040830/lite-20250628.htm), $303.9 million in FY2025, and $252.1 million in the nine months ended March 2026—at approximately 18 to 22 percent of revenue in down years, declining as a percentage as cloud-and-datacenter revenues accelerate. The sustained spend, even through the FY2023–FY2024 telecom trough when revenue fell to $1.36 billion, preserved the engineering teams whose EML yield improvements and 200G chip advances are now translating directly into gross margin expansion.

chapters.title: AI datacom durability, Coherent competition, hyperscaler concentration, China exposure
chapters.body:
The six risks that shadow Lumentum's Hurlston-era repositioning share a common topology: each is structural enough to withstand a good quarterly print but specific enough to reward investors who weight them carefully. They range from the macro-cyclical to the geopolitical, but all six ultimately come back to the same question — whether a company that compressed from $1.74 billion in fiscal 2023 revenue to $1.36 billion in fiscal 2024 has genuinely found a durable floor under the cloud-and-datacenter business, or merely traded one concentration risk for another.

## AI Datacom Cycle Sustainability

The most consequential risk in the Lumentum thesis is not whether 800G transceivers sell, but whether the hyperscaler buildout sustains the velocity at which they are ordered. The company's cloud-and-datacenter revenue inflection through fiscal 2024 and into fiscal 2025 rested on a capital expenditure supercycle at Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta — entities whose infrastructure spending is large, lumpy, and subject to sudden digestion periods. [Lumentum investor relations](https://investor.lumentum.com) filings consistently described the category as driven by AI-related optical interconnect demand, yet they also consistently avoided forward guidance extending more than a quarter.

The structural mitigants are meaningful. Optical transceiver content per rack unit rises with each generation: the step from 400G to 800G to the emerging 1.6T represents a roughly proportional increase in the value of optical components per port. If hyperscaler capex pauses but rack densification continues, Lumentum can defend revenue on lower unit volumes. The transition to 1.6T architectures, which Hurlston consistently characterised as beginning its commercial ramp in calendar 2025, provides a product cycle that should refresh the order book even as 800G volumes plateau.

The concern is the inventory dynamics that have already scarred the company once. The fiscal 2024 trough was partly an optical-components-specific inventory correction layered on top of the Apple VCSEL normalisation; cloud customers built safety stock during a capacity-constrained environment and then decelerated orders in concert. That pattern is latent in any demand-driven cycle. Lumentum has limited visibility into end-demand beyond the purchase orders in hand, and the hyperscaler procurement model — concentrated, annual-agreement-driven, subject to architecture reviews — means that a single large customer redirecting spend can move the needle before the income statement reflects it.

## Coherent and Marvell-Inphi Competition

Lumentum's principal merchant competitor in AI datacom transceivers is Coherent Corp — the entity formed when II-VI completed its acquisition of the legacy Coherent Corporation in early 2022 and rebranded the combined business. Coherent brought its own vertical indium phosphide capability through the Finisar acquisition of 2019, and the combined entity offers a product portfolio that spans from the InP chip to the transceiver module level in direct competition with Lumentum's cloud-and-datacenter business. Coherent has also aggressively pursued the same hyperscaler accounts.

Marvell Technology's Inphi unit — acquired in 2021 for approximately $10 billion — represents a different vector. Inphi's PAM4 and coherent DSP silicon increasingly allows systems vendors and hyperscalers to source optics and electronics separately, then integrate internally — potentially commoditising the value that Lumentum captures at the component layer. As hyperscalers mature their co-packaged optics architectures and drive more of the electro-optical integration in-house, the risk is that merchant transceiver suppliers lose pricing power to systems that absorb the optical function into the silicon package.

Lumentum's mitigants are the indium phosphide vertical integration inherited from the December 2018 Oclaro acquisition — a roughly $1.8 billion transaction that secured a Milpitas chip fabrication facility — and the coherent IP from the August 2022 NeoPhotonics deal at approximately $918 million. Together they give the company substrate economics and coherent DSP relationships that a pure-play transceiver assembler could not replicate quickly. The concern is that Coherent Corp has an equivalent or superior InP capability and a larger combined revenue base from which to sustain price competition through a capacity-rich environment.

## Hyperscaler Customer Concentration

Cloud-and-datacenter concentration is simultaneously the source of Lumentum's post-trough recovery and the most legible single-point risk in the equity story. [SEC EDGAR filings for CIK 0001633978](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001633978) have disclosed customer concentration levels consistent with one or two hyperscaler accounts representing meaningful double-digit percentages of total revenue — a structure that creates acute vulnerability to vendor diversification decisions, co-packaged optics architectural shifts, or changes in a single customer's AI capital allocation timeline.

The mitigant most often advanced by the Hurlston team is supply scarcity: diversifying away from Lumentum is genuinely difficult in a constrained InP environment. The Milpitas wafer fabrication line is among the small number of merchant InP chip sources globally, and scaling an alternative supplier to production volumes requires multi-year qualification cycles. The concern is that the constraint is not permanent. Both Coherent Corp and vertically integrated hyperscalers were investing in InP capacity as of early 2026, and the moat that appeared deep during a tight-supply period narrows proportionally as the industry adds capacity to meet AI interconnect demand.

## China and Thailand Geopolitical Exposure

Lumentum's manufacturing footprint carries two distinct geopolitical exposures that the Hurlston team inherited rather than created. The first is a Thailand-based manufacturing operation — a legacy of the Oclaro acquisition — that handles volume optical component production. Thailand is not a sanctions target, but it sits within regional supply chains whose logistics, labour markets, and tariff treatment are subject to the collateral effects of the US-China trade framework. Any escalation in South-east Asian trade policy — tightened rules-of-origin enforcement, revised tariff schedules under US trade law — creates cost and continuity risk that the company has limited ability to hedge in the short term.

The second, more acute exposure is China itself. Lumentum sold into Chinese telecom OEMs and maintained China-sourced components in its supply chain. US export controls on optical and photonic components expanded significantly after 2022, and the trajectory of those controls — which the Commerce Department periodically tightened around semiconductor-adjacent photonics — created both direct revenue risk if Chinese customers became restricted and compliance cost if the supply chain required restructuring. The compounding risk is incremental: no single enforcement action necessarily impairs the business materially, but successive tightening progressively narrows both the addressable market and the cost-efficient supply base simultaneously.

## Telecom Recovery Trajectory

The telecom business — Lumentum's original core — entered a severe downturn in 2023 as tier-1 OEMs including Cisco, Ciena, Nokia, Ericsson, and Infinera digested inventory accumulated during the post-pandemic components shortage. Revenue from the telecom category fell sharply through fiscal 2023 and into fiscal 2024, contributing meaningfully to the trough at $1.36 billion. By the fiscal 2025 reporting period, the segment had stabilised off the bottom, but the recovery pace remained the principal uncertainty.

Lumentum's structural mitigant is that ROADM and coherent transceiver content in deployed carrier networks defers rather than disappears. When carriers return to network build, optical layer component demand follows mechanically. The NeoPhotonics coherent IP positions the company for the 400ZR and 800ZR coherent transceiver standards that underpin long-haul and metro network upgrades. The concern is timing and slope. Carrier capex has been persistently restrained since the 2022 peak, and there is no external catalyst analogous to the AI forcing function that drove datacom demand. The telecom recovery appears more likely to trace a multi-year gradient than a V-shaped snapback — meaning that the segment may recover its prior revenue contribution too slowly to offset any moderation in the cloud-and-datacenter growth rate.

## Commercial Lasers Cyclical Exposure

The Commercial Lasers segment serves industrial manufacturers using high-power fiber lasers for cutting, welding, and additive manufacturing, as well as semiconductor equipment makers including ASML and Applied Materials. These demand pools carry distinct cyclicalities that rarely align with the optical communications business. Industrial laser demand tracks manufacturing activity and capital goods spending, both sensitive to global trade conditions; semiconductor equipment demand tracks advanced logic and memory node investment cycles, which compressed sharply in 2023-2024 before recovering into 2025-2026.

The mitigant is a structural linkage to AI infrastructure that Hurlston's team has consistently emphasised: advanced packaging, chiplet architectures, and heterogeneous integration all require precision laser processing equipment, and Lumentum supplies laser sources into that toolset. The concern is competitive exposure. Commercial Lasers is a smaller, structurally less defensible revenue stream than optical communications — one where Lumentum competes against IPG Photonics and others without the same InP-derived moat. Margin profiles in the segment are more exposed to pricing pressure in a soft industrial environment, and a prolonged manufacturing slowdown could suppress the segment at the same time that telecom recovery delays and AI datacom digestion combine to pressure the optical communications line. The diversification value of Commercial Lasers is real; the segment's capacity to offset an optical communications disappointment is limited.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The closing fiscal year and the next four quarters

Lumentum reached the May 2026 snapshot with its fiscal 2026 year in its final weeks. The fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 — closing around late June or early July 2026, with results expected in August 2026 — will deliver the first full-year P&L scorecard on Michael Hurlston's cloud-and-datacenter pivot: a direct comparison against the $1.36 billion fiscal 2024 trough and the first real test of whether the 800G transceiver volume at hyperscaler customers had driven a durable structural recovery or a cyclical bounce.

The August 2026 earnings call was, at the snapshot date, the most important near-term event on the calendar. Beyond the quarterly figures, management was expected to initiate fiscal 2027 guidance and provide the first granular framing of 1.6T transceiver contribution timing — the variable on which the forward consensus most depends.

## The catalyst timeline: Q4 FY2026 through Q3 FY2027

**Q4 FY2026 (July 2026 close, August 2026 report).** The inflection confirmation quarter. The consensus watch point was cloud-and-networking revenue holding sequential momentum from the growth trajectory established across Q1–Q3 FY2026. Gross margin recovery toward the mid-30s non-GAAP range — the threshold at which InP vertical integration begins to generate visible operating leverage at scale — was the secondary diagnostic. An August 2026 call that paired cloud-and-networking revenue above the high end of guidance with a gross margin at or above 35% non-GAAP would constitute the clearest available validation of the post-trough model.

**Q1 FY2027 (October 2026 close, November 2026 report).** The seasonality test. First quarters of Lumentum's fiscal year have historically carried the risk of hyperscaler capex lumpiness — orders that front-load in the spring and leave a digestion gap in the summer and early autumn. The November 2026 call will establish whether the 800G demand signal at Lumentum's cloud customers is structural or whether inventory digestion produces a sequential revenue step-down. Any management commentary on customer order visibility extending twelve or more months would be a notably positive signal.

**Q2 FY2027 (January 2027 close, February 2027 report).** The 1.6T checkpoint. By Q2 FY2027, Lumentum's 1.6T transceiver qualification work at hyperscaler customers — led by Téa Williams's cloud-and-networking organisation — was expected to be sufficiently mature to generate either a design-win disclosure or a production-ramp commitment. The February 2027 call is the earliest plausible date for a 1.6T revenue contribution announcement, and any language shift from "customer qualification" to "production ramp" would be a material forward catalyst.

**Q3 FY2027 (April 2027 close, May 2027 report).** The full-year visibility anchor. By the third quarter, management typically has sufficient pipeline visibility to narrow FY2027 full-year guidance meaningfully. If 1.6T is contributing volume revenue and 800G volumes have held through the seasonal period, Q3 FY2027 could represent the first quarter in which Lumentum's quarterly run-rate implies a full-year revenue profile meaningfully above the fiscal 2023 pre-trough level of approximately $1.74 billion.

## Consensus estimates: the forward grid

The following table reflects approximate sell-side consensus expectations as of the May 2026 snapshot date. Lumentum does not provide multi-quarter guidance; the figures are market estimates, not company guidance.

| Period | Quarter End | Revenue (consensus, approx.) | Non-GAAP EPS (approx.) | Implied YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 FY2026 | Late June/July 2026 | ~$490–510M | ~$0.55–0.65 | ~35–40% |
| Q1 FY2027 | Late Sept/Oct 2026 | ~$480–505M | ~$0.50–0.60 | ~30–35% |
| Q2 FY2027 | Late Dec/Jan 2027 | ~$510–540M | ~$0.60–0.75 | ~28–33% |
| Q3 FY2027 | Late March/April 2027 | ~$545–580M | ~$0.72–0.88 | ~27–32% |
| **FY2027 Full Year** | **Late June/July 2027** | **~$2.10–2.25B** | **~$2.75–3.30** | **~18–24%** |

The implied fiscal 2026 full-year consensus of approximately $1.85–1.95 billion represented a recovery of roughly 36–43% from the $1.36 billion fiscal 2024 trough. The fiscal 2027 consensus of $2.10–2.25 billion implied a further 15–20% step-up, principally from sustained 800G volumes at hyperscalers plus an assumed emerging 1.6T contribution in the back half of the fiscal year.

## The three metrics that matter most

The quarterly dashboard for the next twelve months reduces to three discriminating metrics.

**Cloud-and-networking revenue — absolute level and sequential direction.** This is the primary P&L line for the thesis. Sequential declines beyond seasonal norms in Q1 FY2027 would be the earliest warning signal of either hyperscaler inventory digestion or competitive share loss. A hold-or-grow sequential pattern across Q1 through Q3 FY2027 would be the strongest available confirmation of structural demand.

**Non-GAAP gross margin.** The 35% threshold is the visible inflection point at which InP vertical integration's fixed-cost structure begins generating operating leverage at current volumes. A trajectory toward 37–38% gross margin by fiscal 2027's second half would indicate that 800G scale has moved into the zone where Lumentum's integration advantage compounds. A trajectory that stalls below 34% would raise structural questions about pricing pressure or competitive intensity from Coherent Corporation.

**1.6T qualification and production language.** Hurlston's cloud-and-networking team has consistently framed 1.6T in qualification terms rather than production-commitment terms. The linguistic transition — from "qualification progressing with our customer base" to "production ramp underway" — will precede the revenue contribution by one to two quarters and represents the highest-value signal the earnings calls can deliver in the forward window. Any indication that qualification timelines have extended would be a negative read-through.

## Beat versus miss: the decision matrix

A beat against Q4 FY2026 consensus would require cloud-and-networking revenue at or above the high end of management guidance, non-GAAP gross margin at or above 35%, and either a 1.6T design-win disclosure or language indicating that production timing had been committed with a specific hyperscaler customer. Given the revenue-to-EPS operating leverage at this scale, an EPS beat is essentially a derivative outcome of the margin and revenue combination.

A miss would be signalled by cloud-and-networking revenue below the guidance midpoint — indicating hyperscaler capex timing slippage or share loss — gross margin compressing below 33%, or any management language that softened the 1.6T production timeline from the prior quarter's framing. A two-consecutive-quarter revenue miss against consensus would substantially compress the forward multiple.

## The asymmetry: bull and bear into fiscal 2027

The bull case rests on two compounding factors. First, 800G volumes at hyperscaler customers sustain through fiscal 2027 without a material inventory digestion quarter — plausible given the publicly disclosed multi-hundred-billion-dollar AI infrastructure capital expenditure commitments from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta across the 2026–2027 horizon. Second, 1.6T enters production in the first half of fiscal 2027, adding an incremental revenue layer on top of maintained 800G volumes. In this scenario, fiscal 2027 revenue could reach $2.3–2.5 billion with non-GAAP EPS above $4.00, placing the stock on a sub-15x forward earnings multiple — a re-rating catalyst consistent with the company's indium phosphide vertical integration moat and the absence of a credible merchant InP alternative at scale.

The bear case centres on three risks, each of which has precedent in the optical components sector. Hyperscaler capex lumpiness — the front-loading and subsequent digestion pattern — has generated air-pocket quarters repeatedly across the sector's history, and Lumentum is not structurally immune regardless of InP integration advantages. A two-quarter digestion period at a single major hyperscaler customer could compress fiscal 2027 revenue by $100–150 million against consensus. The second risk is competitive displacement by Coherent Corporation, which has been investing in InP capacity and coherent transceiver scale. The third risk is 1.6T timing slippage: if customer qualifications extend by two quarters, the revenue contribution embedded in fiscal 2027's second half slides entirely into fiscal 2028, removing a growth premium that current consensus already prices.

The asymmetry as of May 2026 modestly favoured the bull case, given that 800G demand from hyperscalers had sustained longer than the bear scenario had anticipated at the start of the 2024–2025 cycle. But the optical components sector has consistently punished excess optimism, and the inventory digestion risk is never fully priced until it materialises in a quarterly result. The next twelve months will test whether Hurlston's cloud-and-datacenter pivot — assembled on the InP foundation of the 2018 Oclaro acquisition and the coherent technology base of the 2022 NeoPhotonics deal — has produced the durable, diversified revenue structure the decade of acquisitions was ultimately assembled to enable.

chapters.title: 1.6T scaling, Hurlston operational restructuring, and the FY2027 horizon
chapters.body:
## The 800G ramp matures

By the spring of 2026, Lumentum's cloud-and-datacenter segment had spent roughly six consecutive quarters absorbing the force of the 800G transceiver cycle, and the revenue trajectory showed it. The company's fiscal 2024 — the year ending late June 2024 — marked what analysts had begun calling the trough: approximately $1.36 billion in total revenue, compressed from the post-Apple-VCSEL peak years and compounded by a synchronised telecom market downturn that had punished most optical components names through 2023. What followed under Michael Hurlston, who assumed the chief executive role in February 2024 after a tenure at Synaptics and earlier work at Broadcom's mobile connectivity division, was a studied effort to redirect the company's considerable manufacturing assets toward the most durable demand signal visible in the optical components industry — the AI datacenter buildout.

The pace of 800G shipments to hyperscaler customers accelerated materially through Lumentum's fiscal 2025, with the cloud-and-datacenter category becoming the dominant revenue driver at the expense of the legacy telecom and Apple VCSEL mix that had defined the company through much of the 2019–2023 period. [Investor Relations, Lumentum](https://investor.lumentum.com) The trajectory reflected both Lumentum's structural advantage — the indium phosphide vertical integration acquired through the December 2018 Oclaro deal at roughly $1.8 billion — and the deliberate capacity decisions Hurlston and his team made to prioritise the AI-linked transceiver lines over lower-margin commodity alternatives.

## Hurlston's operational restructuring

Hurlston arrived with a reputation for financial discipline cultivated at Synaptics, where he had engineered margin expansion through a combination of portfolio rationalisation and manufacturing cost reduction. He applied analogous logic at Lumentum with unusual speed. Within his first three quarters as chief executive, the company announced headcount and facilities actions that the management team framed as positioning Lumentum for the next phase of growth rather than a defensive contraction.

> "We are building an organisation that can scale with the hyperscaler opportunity without carrying the structural cost base that was designed for a different era of the business."

That framing — restructuring as forward investment rather than retreat — ran through the company's earnings communications consistently through fiscal 2025. The actions targeted both the commercial lasers segment, where industrial end-market softness had persisted, and legacy telecom-facing operations where the prolonged inventory digestion cycle had left capacity underutilised. The restructuring charges were material in the near term but the stated aim was a leaner operating model capable of generating meaningful operating leverage as 800G volumes climbed and as 1.6T sampling revenue began to accrue.

Gross margin recovery was a central metric of the Hurlston-era narrative. From the compressed levels of fiscal 2024 — when revenue dilution from underutilised InP fabs and the telecom trough combined — the trajectory through fiscal 2025 and into fiscal 2026 showed progressive improvement as the cloud-and-datacenter mix shift worked in the company's favour and as the restructuring actions reduced the fixed-cost burden.

## The 1.6T roadmap

The transition from 800G to 1.6T Ethernet transceiver standards represented the most consequential near-term product cycle question facing Lumentum in the 2025–2026 window. Hyperscaler fabric architectures had continued to evolve rapidly, driven by the compute density requirements of large language model training clusters, and the 1.6T specification — built on 200G-per-lane optical engines — was advancing toward qualification timelines that placed initial volume revenue in fiscal 2026 and meaningful scale in fiscal 2027.

Lumentum's position in the 1.6T cycle rested on the same indium phosphide manufacturing depth that had differentiated it at 800G. The company's San Jose and NeoPhotonics-heritage facilities gave it wafer-level control over the optical chip sets that define transceiver cost and performance at 200G-per-lane — a capability that pure-play packaging houses and several fabless competitors could not replicate from merchant InP supply given continued global InP capacity constraints.

> "The 1.6T design wins we are pursuing today determine our revenue position in fiscal '27. We are engaged with every meaningful hyperscaler customer on qualification."

Sampling and early qualification activity with lead hyperscaler customers was underway through the first half of calendar 2026. The company was careful to distinguish between design-win engagement — which it characterised as broad — and qualified, awarded programmes converting to purchase orders, which it described as progressing on plan. The NeoPhotonics coherent technology, acquired in August 2022 for approximately $918 million, contributed integrated coherent optics capability relevant to the longer-reach variants of 1.6T for campus and metro datacenter interconnect, extending Lumentum's addressable surface beyond the short-reach pluggable market.

## Telecom stabilisation

After the prolonged downturn that suppressed telecom capital expenditure through 2023 and much of 2024, the segment showed nascent signs of stabilisation by Lumentum's fiscal 2025 second half. ROADM shipments to major OEM customers — Cisco, Nokia, Ericsson, Ciena, and Infinera collectively — had absorbed the worst of the inventory correction, and order patterns by early fiscal 2026 pointed to normalisation rather than further compression.

Telecom, however, was no longer the growth engine Lumentum's management team was prepared to bet on structurally. Hurlston's communications consistently characterised telecom as a stable, profitable cash-flow contributor within a portfolio reweighted toward datacom. The ROADM line card and tunable laser business retained competitive position and solid customer relationships; it simply competed for internal capital allocation against a cloud-and-datacenter opportunity growing faster at higher incremental margins.

## Commercial lasers: the lagging cycle

The commercial lasers segment — industrial cutting and welding lasers, plus the semiconductor equipment lasers supplied to customers including ASML and Applied Materials — remained a study in cyclical lag through the first half of fiscal 2026. Industrial laser demand tracked global manufacturing capex, which had not yet recovered meaningfully from the 2023–2024 investment pause among European and North American manufacturers. Semiconductor equipment exposure offered some insulation given the ongoing CHIPS Act–driven fab construction wave in the United States, but that revenue line was smaller in absolute terms.

Hurlston's restructuring actions explicitly addressed the commercial lasers cost base, and management communications framed a recovery in the segment as incremental upside rather than a prerequisite for the FY2027 margin targets. The segment's profitability was real and its customer relationships durable; the timing of the industrial capex recovery remained, as of the frozen snapshot window in late May 2026, difficult to call with precision.

## Risks revisited

| Risk factor | Status as of May 2026 |
|---|---|
| Customer concentration (hyperscaler 1–2) | Persistent; mitigated by multi-cloud engagement and 1.6T design-win breadth |
| InP supply / capacity | Structural advantage; risk is execution at scale as 1.6T volumes ramp |
| Competitive entry (II-VI/Coherent, Sumitomo, POET) | Intensifying; InP vertical integration remains differentiator |
| Telecom cycle duration | Stabilising; not a growth driver on current management roadmap |
| Apple VCSEL dependency | Structurally moderated; consumer 3D sensing is a diminishing share of the mix |
| FX and geopolitical supply chain | Thailand and San Jose manufacturing mitigates PRC risk; Taiwan InP concentration residual |
| Gross margin recovery pace | On trajectory; risk is 1.6T start-up costs and 800G pricing pressure |

The competitive dynamics in the 800G-and-beyond optical transceiver market had sharpened materially. II-VI's absorption into Coherent produced a better-resourced competitor with its own vertical integration ambitions. Sumitomo Electric and Mitsubishi Electric retained formidable InP positions. At the fabless or lighter-fab end, POET Technologies and several Taiwan-based assembly-heavy competitors were attempting to close the cost gap on Lumentum's integrated model. Hurlston acknowledged the pressure without conceding the structural argument:

> "We compete on the full vertical stack. That is not a marketing statement — it is a manufacturing reality that takes years and capital to replicate."

## The durability question

The dossier closes on the question any serious analyst of Lumentum must ultimately answer: how durable is the cloud-and-datacenter growth franchise once the 800G-to-1.6T transition is complete and hyperscalers have digested their initial AI cluster builds?

The honest answer, available from the evidence assembled through the May 2026 window, is constructively ambiguous. The structural argument for Lumentum is compelling: every generation of compute scaling has historically generated more optical interconnect content per rack, not less, and the move to 800G and then 1.6T represented an acceleration of that trend rather than a reversal. Lumentum's indium phosphide depth means its competitive moat is widest precisely where the bandwidth-per-watt requirements are most stringent — the short-reach, high-density intra-cluster links that define AI datacenter architecture.

The risk argument is equally real. Hyperscaler capex is lumpy, and the optical component supply chain has demonstrated in multiple prior cycles that inventory digestion can arrive faster than manufacturers anticipate. The 2023–2024 trough — Lumentum's $1.36 billion fiscal year — was a reminder that no structural advantage fully insulates a components supplier from a customer inventory correction.

What Hurlston's first two years as chief executive had assembled, by May 2026, was a company with a lower structural cost base, an advancing 1.6T design-win portfolio, and a management culture visibly more focused on operating discipline than its predecessor regime had been. Whether that translated to a fiscal 2027 that justified the investor optimism baked into the share price remained, at the close of this frozen snapshot, the open question on which the next chapter of the Lumentum story would turn.

---

## Appendix C — Principal Product Categories

**Optical Communications** (largest segment): datacom transceivers including 800G and emerging 1.6T pluggables for cloud-and-datacenter applications; coherent transceivers for telecom and long-haul; ROADMs (reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers) for metro and long-haul networks; indium phosphide chips and modules; VCSELs (vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers) primarily for 3D sensing applications.

**Commercial Lasers**: fibre lasers and diode lasers for industrial manufacturing applications; solid-state and ultrafast lasers for semiconductor equipment and precision manufacturing OEMs including ASML and Applied Materials.

---

## Appendix D — Principal Customer Categories

**Cloud and Datacenter**: Hyperscaler cloud providers consuming 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers for AI and general datacenter interconnect. The cloud-and-datacenter category was the primary revenue growth driver through the 2024–2025 period under Hurlston.

**Telecom OEMs**: Cisco, Nokia, Ericsson, Ciena, Infinera, and comparable network equipment manufacturers consuming ROADMs, coherent transceivers, and related optical components for carrier infrastructure.

**3D Sensing / Consumer**: Apple historically consumed VCSELs for Face ID and related 3D sensing applications; this revenue stream moderated substantially through the FY2024 trough period.

**Industrial and Semiconductor Equipment**: Trumpf, IPG Photonics (as competitive reference), ASML, Applied Materials, and comparable OEMs consuming fibre and solid-state lasers.

---

## Appendix E — Competitive References

**Coherent Corp. (COHR)**: The principal listed merchant optical components competitor following Coherent's 2022 merger with II-VI Incorporated. Coherent and Lumentum compete across datacom transceivers, coherent telecom modules, and indium phosphide chip supply.

**Marvell Technology / Inphi**: Marvell acquired Inphi Corporation in 2021 for approximately $10 billion, establishing a competing silicon photonics and high-speed interconnect position relevant to the 800G transceiver ecosystem.

**Chinese transceiver vendors**: InnoLight, Eoptolink, HG Genuine, and comparable China-based transceiver manufacturers have competed on price for datacenter pluggable volumes, creating margin pressure in the standard-reach 800G market while Lumentum's indium phosphide integration anchors positioning in higher-performance segments.
